en: The Scripture on the Questions of the Brahma-Devaputra Cittadhara, Scroll One. Also titled *The Adornment of the Meaning of All Buddha-Dharmas*, or alternatively *The Scripture Spoken by the Buddha on the Equal Mastery of All Dharmas*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Radiance of the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha at the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus—sixty-four thousand bhikṣus—and seventy-two thousand bodhisattvas. All were great sages who had perfected their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), attained dhāraṇīs, possessed unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*), and were firmly established in samādhi. Their wisdom was fearless, they thoroughly understood the spontaneous nature of all phenomena, and had attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Their names were as follows: [The list of names follows]... (and so forth).

The youth Viśiṣṭacāritra, the youth Ratnakāra, the youth Ratnamudrāhasta, the youth Ratnaśīrṣa, the youth Gaganagañja, the youth Saṃcodanasaddharmacakrapravartin, the youth Jālinīprabha, the youth Sarvāvaraṇaviskambhin, the youth Sarvadada, the youth Jayagarbha, the youth Padmacārin, the youth Siṃha, the youth Candraprabha, the youth Āśaya, and the youth Svālaṃkāra.
The sixteen noble beings, such as Bhadrapāla, Ratnakara, Guhagupta,

Indradatta, Varuṇadatta, Bhadrajita, Uttaramati, Dharmamati, Viśeṣamati, Susīma, Amoghadarśin, Anikṣiptadhura, Akṣayamati, Sūdgata, Sūryagarbha, and Dharanidhara— of such a kind, there were seventy-two thousand.

The Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra and his retinue, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven;

the various Brahmā deities, including those of the Brahmakāyika Heaven and other celestial beings, together with nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all came to assemble there.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a retinue of countless hundreds of thousands of beings as he preached the Dharma.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Instantly, he caused the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system to tremble, raining down a profusion of various flowers upon the assembled multitude. He addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I humbly ask the Perfectly Awakened One!”
"It is the destination of the ignorant;
if you will compassionately grant me an audience, I shall venture to speak.
The Buddha told Jālinīprabha:
“Ask whatever you desire; for all those who are deluded, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, shall provide an explanation to bring joy to your hearts.
Having received permission to inquire, Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!”

The Tathāgata’s physical form and radiance are difficult to withstand, surpassing the brilliance of the sun by hundreds of thousands of millions of times; his countenance and majestic authority are unapproachable, such that from the highest heavens to the lowest depths none can gaze upon him clearly; the practices he has established and cultivated are beyond all measure.
Furthermore, I thought to myself:

"Whoever is able to behold the physical form of the Most True One and contemplate his deeds is touched by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, the Great Sage; whatever they set forth shall immediately lead them to eternal peace."
The World-Honored One said:
“Bodhisattva Net of Radiance!

It is exactly as you have said; one who beholds the body of the Tathāgata will certainly attain their aspirations and not fail in their expectations. If there is anything you wish to ask, it shall be likewise.”
He then addressed Jālinīprabha:

"The World-Honored One possesses a light named 'Silent Discourse. If sentient beings encounter this radiance and behold the Tathāgata, they will observe his form and color with such clarity of the visual faculty that it shall never again be obscured by darkness."
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Fearless Eloquence"; if one encounters this light, one is capable of questioning the Tathāgata regarding the destination of difficult inquiries.

Moreover, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Accumulated Virtuous Merit"; if one encounters this light, one is able to inquire of the Buddha concerning all the virtuous deeds of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Pure Clarity"; if one encounters this light, one is able to question the Buddha regarding the causes and conditions for the birth of Śakra.
Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Attaining the Blazing Lamp"; if one encounters this light, one is able to question the Buddha regarding the birth in the Brahma Heaven.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Door of Liberation from the Dusts of Desire"; if one encounters this light, one is able to inquire of the Buddha regarding the vehicle of the śrāvaka.

Moreover, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Single-minded Adherence to Austerities"; if one encounters this light, one is able to inquire of the Buddha regarding the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Upholding the Praise of All-Wisdom. Should one encounter this light, one will be able to inquire of the Buddha regarding the wisdom of the Mahāyāna and the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Joyful Sustenance of Steadfast Steps. Should one encounter this light, wherever the Tathāgata wanders or paces, all shall obtain universal peace and security; after the end of their life, they shall attain rebirth in the heavens.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named Adorned with All Pure Garlands; whenever the Tathāgata enters a city and emits this radiance, all who encounter it attain peace, and at that moment, the various precious garlands of that city spontaneously become adorned.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Destruction and Removal. Should the Tathāgata manifest this light, it would shake countless and immeasurable Buddha-worlds.
"To state the essentials: furthermore, Jālinīprabha!
The light of the Tathāgata is called 'Accumulated Peace. If those belonging to the class of hell-beings encounter this light, their manifold afflictions and sufferings will naturally cease."
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Transcending Compassion"; if birds and beasts encounter this light, they will never again give rise to malice or harm one another.
Moreover, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Relieving What Is Created"; if the various classes of hungry ghosts encounter this light, they will no longer suffer from hunger or thirst.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Free from Defilement"; if those who are blind encounter this radiance, they shall regain their sight.
Moreover, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Hearing with the Ear"; those who are deaf shall be able to hear upon encountering this light.
"Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called 'Possessing Resolve'; if one encounters this light, those who are distracted attain correctness.
Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called 'Joyous Lamp'; if one encounters this light, one naturally reforms evil and establishes the ten wholesome actions."
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Gate of Liberation"; encountering this radiance causes those with false views to attain right view.
Moreover, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Ascent to Heaven"; those who encounter this light cause those of avaricious and greedy nature to delight in giving.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Free from Torment"; if one encounters this light, those who have committed evil will uphold the prohibitive precepts.
Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Sustaining the Mind"; through it, those who harbor anger and resentment attain patience.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Diligence," by which those who are indolent attain vigor.
Moreover, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Right Concentration," by which those who are heedless achieve meditative absorption.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Radiant Brilliance," by which those of evil wisdom attain clever discernment.
Moreover, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Pure Clarity," by which those who harbor doubts attain firm faith.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Dhāraṇī," which causes those of little wisdom to attain extensive learning.
Moreover, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Following the Traces of Words," which causes those who lack a sense of shame to attain a sense of modesty.
Furthermore, there is a Tathāgata light named "Extinguishing," which washes away the emotional states of those who are lustful.
Moreover, there is a Tathāgata light named "Peace and Bliss," which causes those who harbor anger to be free from wrath and malice.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Illuminating," which causes those who practice through delusion to eliminate their ignorance and darkness.
Moreover, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Universal Preservation," which causes those who follow the equal-parts temperament to completely relinquish that equal-parts disposition.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Universally Manifesting Physical Form. If sentient beings encounter this radiance, they shall behold the infinite colors of all Tathāgatas and their incalculable hundreds of thousands of forms.
The Buddha told Jālinīprabha:

"Now I have merely outlined the essentials for you. Even if one were to spend an eon, or even more than an eon, praising and expounding upon the Tathāgata’s radiance and discussing and elucidating the Dharma of the sutras, one could not exhaustively describe the Tathāgata’s radiance or the names of its manifestations."
The Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“It is truly unprecedented, O God among Gods!

The body of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, and his sublime virtues are inconceivable. He expounds the Dharma through skillful means according to what is appropriate; that which we had never heard before, we now receive as a blessing.”
Any bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this name of the light, rejoice and believe with delight, shall all attain a body like that of the Tathāgata, majestic and fully endowed.

Furthermore, I have heard that the World-Honored One has manifested the light of all Tathāgatas, named "Exhortation and Transformation. All the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwelling in other lands and foreign realms are being successively urged and inspired by one another; having been thus urged, they are all led to assemble here in this Sahā world. Any Bodhisattva who wishes to inquire or seek instruction shall proceed to the Tathāgata to discuss and resolve their doubts regarding the sutras.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing what the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha had requested, immediately emitted a bodily radiance corresponding to that request, which universally illuminated immeasurable Buddha-lands and incalculable worlds of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, that radiance summoned countless billions of bodhisattvas, who soon gathered in the Sahā world.

At that time, seventy-two thousand Buddha-worlds to the east of here was a land named Pure; its Buddha was named Candraprabha Tathāgata. In that Buddha’s land there was a Brahmā named Mind-Holder (*Cittadhara*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva who was non-retrogressive and who delighted in the power of his own noble wisdom and spiritual faculties.

At that time, having just finished exhorting them, that radiance proceeded in person to where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Candrasūryapradīpa was, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"

I wish to go to the Sahā world to pay homage to, serve, and consult with the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni; I wish to prostrate before him, attend to his needs, and receive his answers to my questions, for the Holy One of the Sahā world also wishes to see me.
That Buddha said to him:
"Go then, Brahmā! You should know that now is the time;
together with an immeasurable billions of bodhisattvas, proceed at once to the Sahā world."
He further said:
"Brahmā! Although you have reached the Sahā world, you must immediately practice the ten types of resolute conduct."
What are the ten? One should accept words—whether they be well-spoken or ill-spoken, beneficial or not beneficial—this is the first;
and one should practice compassion, this is the second.
Third, treating those who are lowly, middling, or superior with equal care;
fourth, directing one's mind with single-mindedness whether encountering contempt or respect;
fifth, not observing the faults of others nor seeking out their blemishes.
Sixth, to regard the various vehicles as being of one single flavor;
seventh, to fear the sound of evil destinies and the wicked;
eighth, to conceive the thought of all bodhisattvas as benefactors.
Ninth, to perceive the Buddha’s land within the world of the five turbidities;
tenth, to see the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as if he were present—
these are the ten matters.
The Buddha said,
“Brahmā! One who harbors such an aspiration and disposition may travel to that land.”
Thereupon, Dhṛtimati addressed the Perfectly Awakened One:

“In the presence of the Buddha, I did not dare utter a sound as a lion’s roar, nor did I manifest extraordinary signs through conditioned activities; I only desired to purify the practice of my own resolute nature, establishing equanimity of mind before traveling to that land.”
Then the other bodhisattvas of the Buddha Candraprabha praised him in verse, saying:
"We have attained a great benefit!
Indeed it is so, World-Honored One!"
"To ensure that they do not give rise to such realms upon attaining auspicious joy, it is because the afflictions, hardships, and labors of sentient beings are thus accumulated.
The World-Honored One Candraprabha addressed the bodhisattvas:
"O sons of noble family!"
Do not speak such words. Why is this?

To practice the pure conduct of Brahma for hundreds of thousands of kalpas in my land is not as good as not giving rise to a single thought of malice from dawn until the mealtime in the Sahā world; the latter is far more excellent.
At that time, twelve thousand bodhisattvas from that land made a vow together, saying:

"We shall fully perfect our pure resolve and character, and together we shall attend upon and protect the Great Being Brahmā, so that he may go to visit the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni."

The Brahmā Citta, together with twelve thousand bodhisattvas, vanished from that buddha-field in the brief moment it takes a valiant man to extend and contract his right arm; he then appeared in the Sahā world, paid homage to the Buddha Śākyamuni, prostrated himself upon the ground, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Jālinīprabha, saying:
"Do you see the Brahmā Devarāja Citta-dhara? He replied:
“I have seen it,” the Great Sage replied.

“This one who maintains his mind understands skillful means and inquires into all that is obscure or stagnant; he distinguishes the honored Dharma with eloquence that is sublime and wondrous, his name being foremost among the assembly of bodhisattvas. With sincere compassion, he benefits others through the Way and exhorts them toward transformation; wherever he dwells or travels, he brings joy and satisfaction to many.”

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dhṛtamatī and twelve thousand other bodhisattvas, having prostrated themselves in salutation and circumambulated the Buddha three times, each used their supernormal powers to magically create a seat and took their places upon it.
The Brahma-Devaputra Cittadhara joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, praising him in verse:
“His wondrous voice reaches everywhere; His majestic virtue spreads far and wide, heard throughout the ten directions.”
In whatever land they dwell, they behold the Most Victorious Ones; all offer praise for the conduct of the Great Sages!
I abide in a different land, pure and stainless; in that realm, even the name of the evil destinies does not exist.
Having sought and then abandoned such a buddha-field as this, I have come here to cultivate and perfect great compassion.
The sublime wisdom of the Buddhas never diminishes; all Tathāgatas are entirely equal.
From the past until the present, they have subdued their wills and natures; thus protecting and sustaining the lands of all Buddhas,
they establish diverse practices, purifying everything, strictly cultivating the ultimate precepts,
and constantly adhering to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Toward those who harbor malice, one returns with loving-kindness; with such an intention, one becomes extraordinary.
By being able to purify the three types of karma, one accordingly protects body, speech, and mind.
The afflictions of the three realms of existence and the various sufferings and vexations are all extinguished in the present through the Dharma.
If bodhisattvas are born here, they shall never harbor any sense of peril or fear.
The karma that leads to the evil realms, along with the paths above and below, have all been severed.
Should there be any bodhisattvas whose minds feel weary or distressed, they shall govern and protect this true Dharma.
In future ages, wherever they may dwell, they shall not lose their resolve nor depart from wisdom.
Should they purify the bonds of all fetters and the defilements of desire,
they shall protect the Dharma of the Buddha-land and thereby transcend it.
To attain all-encompassing wisdom and uphold the True Dharma— if one were to preach it elsewhere,
it would not be as excellent as preaching this sutra until the time of a meal in this Sahā world; this is truly preeminent and the most supreme.
I have also beheld the world of Wondrous Joy, and furthermore, I have examined the Buddha-land of Peace and Bliss.
Therein, there is no suffering or affliction, nor any sound of manifold calamities; even if one were to cultivate goodness, it would not be considered a defining characteristic of their nature.
Even if one were to sweep away all the dust from a hall and chamber, it is far more difficult to always endure the harms inflicted by the foolish and the wicked;
to use the teachings of the sutras to exhort and transform others, leading them to the Supreme Way—
this is truly most difficult.
One should prostrate before that Unsurpassed Honored One, who practices compassion and delivers others from the laws of toil and suffering.
Regarding the conduct of the Tathāgata: toward those whose hearts harbor poison, he transforms them through the Dharma;
whenever he enters an assembly, he acts as their guide.
Their names are heard throughout the ten directions, and they are unimpeded regarding all dharmas;
like a vast ocean, they therefore expound for others this path of the Buddha.
And the World-Protectors, the various devas, nāgas, and spirits, asuras and gandharvas—
countless in number— all came together here, desiring to seek the meaning of the sutra and to receive its explanation according to their aspirations.
All have come together to this great assembly; may the Buddha, for the sake of all, preach the Dharma.
Should there be any who hear it, their destination shall be auspicious.
Should there be those whose aspirations lie in faith and devotion toward the Teacher, whether they be among the assembly of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—
the Capable One fully understands them all; according to their inclinations, he transforms and guides them,
acting solely for the sake of this host to resolve all their doubts.
Now I urge you forward and petition the Dharma King; for the sake of all sentient beings, I am resolved to seek the Buddha-way.
To establish the words of the Buddha so they are not severed, and to cultivate a heart of compassion as an immeasurable treasure—this is my purpose.
Having attained courageous and immeasurable wisdom, you shall preach this peerless practice for their sake,
according to the inclinations, knowledge, and conduct of those sentient beings.
This is not the domain of the śrāvakas, nor can it be reached by any of the pratyekabuddhas.
We have faith and joy in that which has been delivered by the Most Victorious One; the wisdom of the World-Honored One is inconceivable.
I, a humble person, take refuge in the World’s Teacher; now I wish to inquire of the Great Sage regarding this meaning.
If there be weariness, or if the mind loathes toil and affliction, pray explain for my sake the essential path of the Buddha.

2. Chapter on the Four Dharmas (1). Chapter Two: On the Four Dharmas. Thereupon, after the Brahma-deva Citta had praised the Buddha with these verses, he knelt with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva whose nature and character are firm and strong, and whose mind is neither indolent nor weary?"
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s speech being gentle and their words free from affliction and distress?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s cultivation of roots of virtue surpassing that of all sentient beings?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s deportment being composed and serene rather than abrupt or violent?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s great increase and benefit in pure, white dharmas?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s thorough mastery in traversing the lands they visit?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s employment of skillful means while among sentient beings?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful differentiation and instruction of those among their peers?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s ability to protect the mind of enlightenment?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s exclusive focus on the minds of sentient beings without distraction?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s diligent pursuit of the roots of goodness and abiding in the discourse on the Dharma?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s clear understanding of their thoughts while not abandoning faith?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s transformation of all the various categories of worldly afflictions?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s ability to exercise skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) when entering assemblies?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s expansive propagation, dissemination, and analytical exposition of the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*)?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the power of karmic retribution and the loss of the roots of virtue (*kuśala-mūla*)?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s understanding of the wisdom of non-arising regarding sentient beings and the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā)?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s mastery of skillful means (upāya) while abiding in meditative concentration (dhyāna)?
“What is meant by a bodhisattva not regressing from the teachings of all Buddhas?
What is meant by a bodhisattva never contradicting or doubting the verbal instructions of the Buddhas?
The Buddha addressed the Brahmā Dharmadhara:
“Excellent! Excellent!
It is well that you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a discourse.”
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
"How profound! World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it."
The Brahmā Citta received the instruction and listened attentively.
The Buddha told the Brahmā:
"A bodhisattva possesses four dharmas by which their resolve and nature become firm and strong, remaining without laxity or weariness."
What are these four? They are:
compassion for sentient beings; tireless diligence; regarding all things from beginning to end as like a dream; and the wisdom of the Buddha’s equanimity. These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which what one says is gentle and the words are free from affliction and distress.
What are these four? They are:

the bodhisattva’s single-minded discernment of all phenomena for the sake of a single person; the bodhisattva’s single-minded lack of delight in being born within any of the realms of existence; the bodhisattva’s single-minded praise and exaltation of the Mahāyāna; and the bodhisattva’s single-minded exposition of purity so as not to lose pure karma. These are the four.
“Furthermore, there are four things by which the roots of virtue one cultivates surpass those of all other beings.
What are these four?
They are the observance of precepts, extensive learning, generosity, and renouncing the household life. These are the four.”
"Furthermore, there are four things by which one's deportment is serene and composed, rather than abrupt or violent.
What are these four?
To have no gain, no praise, no fame, and no suffering—these are the four."
"Furthermore, there are four matters that greatly increase the roots of merit within the pure Dharma.
What are these four?

To be fully endowed with the practice of faith and to encourage others; to practice giving without expecting a reward; to nurture and protect the Dharma; and to extensively expound the stages of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*) for the sake of all bodhisattvas—these are the four."
"Furthermore, there are four things by which one reaches the lands where one travels and dwells.
What are these four?
To give rise to the roots of virtue; to cast off all defilements; to understand and encourage others; and to practice with diligent perseverance—these are the four."
“Furthermore, there are four matters concerning the practice of skillful means among sentient beings.

What are these four? To comply with and follow sentient beings; to exhort and transform them toward the roots of virtue; to repent of transgressions and faults; and to explain the Buddha’s work—these are the four.”
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one instructs and transforms those of similar standing.
What are the four?
Compassion for people and things, practicing one's own peace and security, patience and composure, and humility without arrogance—these are the four."
“Furthermore, there are four things that can protect the bodhicitta.
What are these four?

Constantly recollecting the Buddha with one's mind as the root of all virtues; reaching toward the bodhicitta; associating with and drawing near to virtuous friends; and praising the Mahāyāna. These are the four.”
“Furthermore, there are four things that ensure one’s mind remains focused on sentient beings without distraction.

What are these four? Not adopting the mind of a śrāvaka; not adopting the mind of a pratyekabuddha; seeking the Dharma without weariness; and explaining the Dharma as it has been heard to others. These are the four.”
“Furthermore, there are four matters through which one should diligently seek the roots of goodness and abide in the deliberations of the Dharma.
What are these four?

To eliminate all maladies of worldly affliction like a king of physicians; to accord with the roots of virtue without transgression or loss; to contemplate the path in all deliberations to extinguish the suffering of the masses; and to resolve upon the deliberation of Nirvana. These are the four.”
“Furthermore, there are four things by which one clearly understands what is intended and does not abandon faith.
What are these four? They are:

giving rise to the patience of non-arising and transcending the patience of non-extinction; enduring the retribution of dependent origination; enduring that which has no abode; and having no other mind or state of restless striving. These are the four.”
"Furthermore, there are four matters for transforming and guiding those within the realms of worldly afflictions.
What are the four? They are:
maintaining thoughts in accordance with right discourse, upholding the prohibitions and precepts, understanding the power of all dharmas, and delighting in dwelling in seclusion. These are the four."
“Furthermore, there are four matters by which one who enters an assembly can exercise skillful means (*upāya*).
What are these four?

To delight in the discussion of the Dharma without seeking out the faults of others; to practice reverence without arrogance; to seek out virtuous qualities and bestow them upon others rather than for oneself; and to encourage others in the roots of merit one has cultivated. These are the four.”
“Furthermore, there are four matters for expanding and propagating the gift of Dharma, for its circulation and analysis.

What are the four? They are: protecting the True Dharma; transforming oneself and others to cause them to enter into wisdom; practicing the deeds of a true sage; and manifesting the fetters of worldly toil, anger, and resentment. These are the four.”
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which one knows the power of retribution and the loss of the roots of virtue.
What are these four?

Never beholding the faults or deficiencies of others; practicing a mind of loving-kindness to subdue all anger; proclaiming the principle of retribution; and constantly maintaining the aspiration for enlightenment regarding all dharmic activities—these are the four."
“Furthermore, there are four matters for awakening sentient beings to the wisdom of non-arising and the six perfections (ṣaḍpāramitā).
What are these four? They are:

practicing giving without forming factions; transforming others; understanding the four debts of gratitude to transform sentient beings; and delighting in the profound Dharma while conforming to the sūtras. These are the four.”
“Furthermore, there are four matters through which skillful means are fully realized and maintained within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
What are these four?

Discerning the objects of the mind and the destinations of transgressions and merits; exerting effort in the roots of virtue; not abandoning sentient beings; and practicing expedient wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*). These are the four.”
"Furthermore, there are four things by which one does not regress from the Buddha-dharma.
What are these four? They are:

protecting against the perils of immeasurable birth and death; making offerings to and serving countless Buddhas; constantly practicing boundless loving-kindness; and clearly understanding the wisdom of infinite Buddhas. These are the four."
“Furthermore, there are four matters by which one never violates or doubts the teachings of the Buddhas.

What are these four? Not abandoning fundamental wisdom; ensuring that words and deeds correspond; relinquishing heavy greed; and if one establishes anything, doing so while abiding in the fundamental nature. These are the four.”

When the World-Honored One had dispatched [the assembly] and expounded these four matters, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of two Ganges Rivers all resolved their minds upon supreme, perfect enlightenment, and five thousand people attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

These bodhisattvas, who had each come from countless buddha-fields to this assembly, made offerings to the World-Honored One until the entire trichiliocosm was completely covered, with flowers reaching up to their knees.
3. Chapter on the Discernment of Dharma Words (1). Chapter Three: The Discernment of Dharma Words. At that time, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Brahma-king Cittadhara, saying:
"Virtuous One, you have asked about the sublime and honored discourse that accords with the path of skillful means (*upāya*) of the bodhisattvas."
The Buddha spoke in further detail:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva having a matter to inquire about and responding with appropriate deliberation? Dhāraṇīdhara replied:
"To inquire about matters in a manner equal to one's own self is to ask in accordance with reason;
to inquire about the conduct and practices of others in a manner equal [to one's own] is to ask in conformity;
to inquire about the characteristics of the Dharma in a manner equal [to one's own] is to ask in conformity."
Furthermore, Jālinīprabha!
Not reckoning oneself, not reckoning others, and not reckoning phenomena—this is to be in accord with reality.
To inquire about arising, to inquire about cessation, or to inquire about location—these are to be in accord with reality.
If there should be one who asks about the Dharma being without arising or cessation, and regarding conduct in its proper place, that is to be in accord with the truth.
If one asks others about the desires of worldly affliction, or if there is a question concerning strife and inversion, that too is to be in accord with the truth.
"To inquire about birth and death, to inquire about crossing over birth and death, and to inquire about the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—this is to be in accord with reality.
To not inquire about worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), nor about inversion, nor about birth and death, nor about crossing over birth and death, nor about nirvāṇa—this is to be in accord with reality."

Why is this so? Because one who examines all phenomena does not find them to be quiescent; nor does one eliminate the stains of desire, perversions, birth-and-death, or the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), for such would be to conform [to them].
Regarding what is obtained through inquiry, it is to be in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, if there is that which is realized, or if there is that which is eliminated at a specific time, or if there is that which is practiced, it is to be in accordance with reality.

If one does not inquire about what has been attained or realized, if the various perceptions and thoughts are not constrained by time, and if there is no attachment, no notion of elimination, and no view of practice—this is to be in accord with reality.
One raises this question for the sake of all beings; with a mind free from attachment and no intent to dwell upon the question, one acts in accordance with what is appropriate.
If one asks about these various virtuous qualities, it is in accordance with what is appropriate; if one asks about non-virtuous qualities, it is not in accordance with what is appropriate.

"This is a worldly matter; this is a transcendent matter; this is a sinful matter; this is a matter free from sinful karma; this is with outflows; this is with possession; this is without possession. For anyone who raises questions regarding these two categories of matters, one should consider that all such things are not in accordance with the truth."
That which is non-dual and does not perceive dualistic questioning is to be in accord with reality.
To regard all Buddhas as being manifold is to be in accord with reality.
To reckon the dharmas as being manifold is to be in accord with reality.
The various assemblies of noble ones are in accord with what is appropriate for them;
the various sentient beings and various lands are in accord with what is appropriate for them;
the various vehicles of the path and various non-conceptualizations are in accord with what is appropriate for them.
Dharmas have no ownership and possess no diversity; yet to inquire about them through a single principle is to accord with what is appropriate.
All dharmas are as they should be, and all dharmas are without that which is "as they should be."
He further asked the Brahmā:
"What is meant by 'all dharmas being in accord with suchness,' or 'all dharmas not being in accord'?"
He replied: "One who is able to discern [that] all dharmas are, as they should be, dharmas;
even if the mental factors and the mind itself are diligent, one should not follow after them."
To reckon that all phenomena and the characteristics of all dharmas are quiescent, empty, and non-existent is to be in accord with reality.
To not delight in the dharma of stillness is also to be in accord with reality.
"That which is to be performed through this diligent application of effort lies in pride; it is that which is produced, and for one who acts in such a manner, it is likewise as it should be.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'all phenomena being observed'?"
He replied, "When one's own nature is tranquil and at the moment of being free from desire, one contemplates all dharmas.
He then asked the Brahmā:
"Are there few of such a kind who, being unresponsive, do not depart from desire yet accord with the discourse on the Way?
He replied: "O Mingwang! [There are indeed.]”
Many sons and daughters of noble family do not depart from the limit of desire, yet they accord with the Dharma of the discourse on the Path as it truly is.

For those who have already entered and those who are about to enter, there is no entering into the Dharma of wisdom; there is nothing to be attained, there is no person, and there is no one who shall enter.
Why is this so? Did not the World-Honored One of Great Compassion say:

"Those who hear the Dharma taught by the Buddha, if they practice with diligence, shall immediately follow and carry out what has been taught; they shall never again return to worldly lands or dwellings, nor seek after any acquisitions or attainments."
They do not have a destination to which they return; they are neither subject to birth and death, nor do they reach nirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because that which the World-Honored One has realized is that there is neither birth and death, nor is there nirvāṇa.
He asked the Brahmā again:
"Does the Buddha teach the Dharma without transcending the karma of birth and death? He replied:
“World-Honored One, would you not further say of yourself, ‘I have crossed over birth and death’? He replied, “No!”
Therefore, son of good family!
The World-Honored Buddha neither abandons birth-and-death nor seeks nirvana.
If one harbors the conceptualization of birth-and-death and nirvana, then one does not transcend duality.
Since he is without birth and death, what is there to be delivered that would not attain nirvāṇa?
Why is this so? Because he does not view birth and death as unequal [to] nirvāṇa!
The Brahmā replied,
“There is neither birth-and-death, nor is there nirvāṇa.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the Brahmā Dharaṇīdhara, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent, Brahmā!"
"When one wishes to say something, one should speak thus; this is what it means to speak in accordance with reality.

When these words of conformity were spoken, two thousand bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind; for the Brahmā, there was no longer birth-and-death, nor was there nirvāṇa.
The Tathāgata has said:
"He manifests birth and death, yet there is no one who wanders through them; there is neither nirvāṇa nor anything to be grieved for, nor does he perceive any person."

“There is one who has attained parinirvāṇa; even if Brahmā were to enter into this discussion, for such a person there would be neither the phenomenon of birth and death nor the phenomenon of nirvāṇa.
Thereupon, five hundred bhikṣus from the assembly rose from their seats and departed in secret, saying these words:
“We saw that he was pure in his cultivation of the brahma-faring within, and we thought to ourselves:”
"One shall attain extinction, yet there is no one who attains extinction; why then do you, in emptiness, aspire to and study this Way?
Will it truly bring about wisdom?
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
If one were to cause the Dharma to arise [within oneself], then for such a person, a Buddha would not appear in the world, and they would not transcend the perils of birth and death.”
"O God among Gods!
It is for the sake of seeking to see Nirvāṇa.
"Indeed, O God among Gods!"

What is called nirvāṇa is the elimination of all conceptual thoughts; it is not characterized by restless striving, for it is distinct from the various forms of supernatural knowledge (*abhijñā*). If one explains it in such a way, then such bhikṣus are merely deceiving themselves.
“O God among Gods!

One who has gone forth into homelessness within the True Dharma and Vinaya, yet falls into external heterodox views, while still directing his will toward the realm of Nirvāṇa—just as sesame oil, curd, butter, and clarified butter [are produced from milk]—yet extinguishes all phenomena; if such a person attains the eternal parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, I would call that a state of extreme arrogance.”
"O God among Gods!

For one who practices, there is nothing to be practiced; having attained equanimity, they ultimately do not construct or establish any arising phenomena, nor do they seek even their cessation. Furthermore, for one who desires to attain the Dharma, there is no such thing as equanimity."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha said to the Brahmā Cittadhara: "Brahmā, you have spoken thus;

yet when these five hundred bhikṣus heard the Dharma taught, they immediately rose from their seats and departed in secret. Knowing the inclinations of such as these, why do you not lead them into the Dharma?"
"If there are those who have faith and joy, they may thereby be delivered from the net of all views.
Hṛdaya replied, "Noble son!"

If you were to travel to as many Buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges and seek for eons, you would be unable to escape; likewise, from such a semblance-dharma (pratirūpaka-dharma), there is no liberation.
It is like a foolish child who, out of fear of empty space, runs and scatters in every direction, yet cannot escape it.

These bhikṣus are just the same; even if they have attained practices beyond measure, the characteristic of emptiness is natural, the characteristic of signlessness is also natural, and the characteristic of wishlessness is likewise natural.
It is just as if there were another man who sought the void, desiring to obtain the void in the eight directions, above, and below, thinking to himself:
"I wish to obtain the void; I wish to obtain the void."
"Wherever he wishes to travel, his mouth speaks of emptiness yet he does not know emptiness; his speech and his body move through space, yet he does not perceive emptiness.
Thus it is, son of good family!"
These bhikṣus seek nirvāṇa; they practice toward nirvāṇa while seeking nirvāṇa, yet they do not understand that which they have entered.
Why is this? That which is called "attaining nirvāṇa" is merely a provisional designation.
"It is just like space; if there is one who practices in emptiness and travels through space, even what they say is empty. That which is called Nirvana is merely a provisional designation.
When the five hundred bhikṣus heard these words, their outflows were exhausted, their minds were liberated, and they attained supernatural powers. Each of them praised him, saying:
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
All dharmas are already in parinirvāṇa; if there were someone who sought parinirvāṇa, for that person the Buddha would not appear in the world. We, O Great Sage! [say this].

It is not for the sake of ordinary persons, nor is there anything to be learned, nor is there anything not to be learned; there is neither birth-and-death nor nirvana, and no dharma of extinction. Why is this so?
"Furthermore, regarding all supernormal wisdoms, we have already abandoned all paths of wisdom and have brought forth the various Buddha-dharmas.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Have you yourselves already accomplished this and entered into this wisdom to obtain benefit for yourselves?"
He replied, "We have already entered into the realm of afflictions, yet we perform no action.
He asked again:
"For what reason do you say this? The bhikṣus replied, "O Śāriputra!"

If one severs the afflictions yet enters the realm of desire, not wishing for parinirvāṇa—for this reason, we say that they have already entered [the path], performing the afflictions while remaining without action.
Śāriputra said: “Excellent! Excellent!”
"Noble son! You should praise this, for it is the ground of the many blessings established by all you virtuous ones. The bhikṣus said:
“O Śāriputra! Even the World-Honored One, our benevolent lord, is but a benefactor to this impure assembly; how much more so, then, are we who have reached the state of complete purity?
He asked again:
"What does this statement mean?
The bhikṣus replied,
"The Buddha knows that all dharma-realms are fundamentally and entirely pure."
Thereupon, the Brahmā Citta addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘the benefactor of the world’?”
The Buddha told Brahmā:
"One is not deluded by worldly dharmas, nor does one feel shame regarding worldly dharmas.
He then asked the World-Honored One again:
"What is meant by 'having completely purified the deeds that bring merit'? He replied:
"It is because one does not grasp at any phenomena."
He asked again:
"Who is the field of merit for the world? He replied:
"If there is one who does not lose the Buddha-way.
He asked again:
"What is meant by a 'good friend' of sentient beings?"
He replied, “Because I do not abandon any sentient beings.
He asked again:
"Who is it that acts with gratitude toward the Tathāgata?
He replied, "It is one who does not oppose or doubt the Buddha's teachings and commands."
He asked again:
"What is meant by serving the Tathāgata? He replied:
"Because they clearly understand the limit of non-arising.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'approaching the practice of the Tathāgata'?"
He replied, “Because it would be better to lose one’s body and life than to violate the prohibitive precepts.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'reverencing the Tathāgata'?
He replied, "It means that the practitioner maintains and nurtures the sense faculties."
He asked again:
"What is called the great wealth of the world? He replied:
"Because the seven treasures are fully complete.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'knowing contentment within the world'?"
He replied: "Because they have already attained the wisdom that transcends the world.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'thoroughly understanding'? He replied:
"It is because one has no aspirations whatsoever regarding the three realms."
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'admonishing through parables in the world'? He replied:
"Because they have brought rest to all fetters.
He asked again:
"What is meant by dwelling in the world in peace and security?"
He replied, “Because one who is not covetous does not receive wealth.
He asked again:
"What is meant by non-greed?
He replied: "Because there are no hindrances (āvaraṇa) or obscurations (nīvaraṇa)."
He asked again:
"What is meant by being free from the hindrances (āvaraṇa)? He replied:
"Because one abandons the six sense bases and yet there is nothing to be relinquished.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'one's own transgression'?"
He replied, "Because they have clearly understood the wisdom of the Way.
He asked again:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being a master of giving? He replied:
"It is because they exhort and transform all classes of sentient beings, causing them to enter the mind of universal wisdom."
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'prohibitory precepts'? He replied:
"Because they do not abandon the mind of the Way.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'patience' (kṣānti)?"
He replied, "Because I have seen the extinction of the mind.
He asked again:
"What is called diligence? He replied,
"It is because when one seeks it within the mind, no locus can be found."
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'one mind'? He replied:
"Because the mind has come to rest.
He asked again:
"What is meant by wisdom?"
He replied, “Because there is no sound in any phenomenon.
He asked again:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing loving-kindness?
He replied: "Because they do not follow after any conceptualizations."
He asked again:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing compassion? He replied:
"Because there is no recollection of any phenomena.
He asked again:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing joy?"
He replied, "Because I do not conceive of a self.
He asked again:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing protection?
He replied: "Because they do not conceive of the notions of 'self' and 'other'."
He asked again:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva establishing firm and profound faith? He replied:
"Because they do not abandon the purity of all dharmas.
He asked again:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva who is extensively learned and dwells in emptiness?"
He replied, "Because he does not rely upon any sounds.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'shame' (hrī)?
He replied: "It is because of understanding internal phenomena and eliminating [defilements] through that understanding."
He asked again,
"What is meant by 'shame' (hrī)? He replied:
"It is because he does not engage with external phenomena.
He asked the World-Honored One again:
"What is meant by 'the Bodhisattva universally has nothing into which he does not enter'?"
Thereupon, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“His body is pure, refraining from all evils; His speech is pure, always speaking with utmost sincerity;
His mind is pure, constantly practicing a heart of compassion.”
This is called a bodhisattva: universally there is nothing they do not enter.
They do not rely on or become defiled by the dust of the world; they are single-mindedly devoted to compassionate conduct.
They harbor no anger or malice, but instead provide benevolent protection; they are free from delusion. This is called a bodhisattva.
There is nowhere he does not enter.
Whether in market towns, villages, or secluded dwellings, amidst assemblies, there is no distinction;
he never fails in his dignified bearing or ritual propriety. This is what is called a bodhisattva who "enters everywhere without exception."
They have complete and universal faith in the true Dharma of all Buddhas;
they always delight in the scriptures on non-self; they rejoice in the assembly of noble ones;
and they hold no contentious debates—this is called a bodhisattva who universally enters into all things.
Not knowing where one’s actions lead, yet crossing over through anger— yet there is nothing to cross over—
one who clearly understands the destination of all practices is called a bodhisattva;
there is nowhere they do not universally enter.
Nor does one abide within the realm of form; nor is one attached to formlessness—all things are likewise thus.
This is called a bodhisattva who universally penetrates all without exception.
Believing and delighting in all phenomena as entirely empty,
yet seeing sentient beings galloping about in their conceptual thoughts— for this reason, they do not exhaust the outflows.
This is what is called a bodhisattva who universally enters into all things without exception.
Relying on the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, they instruct them through sounds and voices to transform and guide them;
regarding the Great Vehicle of the Buddha, there is nothing they do not thoroughly understand— this is called the Bodhisattva who universally penetrates all.
Never failing the teachings of the Guide, always practicing equanimity toward all who are hateful or dear—
this is called a bodhisattva, who universally enters everywhere.
They never form conceptions regarding past phenomena; the same applies to those of the future and the present.
In all their movements and dwellings, they have no attachments or dependencies;
this is called a bodhisattva who universally penetrates all things.
Thereupon, the Brahmā Citta addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva transcending worldly dharmas?
Without dwelling in worldly dharmas, they manifest entry into the world to deliver and liberate sentient beings.”
Regarding worldly dharmas, he manifests the equality of worldly dharmas;
traversing the world through causes and conditions, although he dwells in the world, he does not subvert worldly dharmas nor lose the dharmas of the Path.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One immediately spoke in verse, responding to Cittahasta:
"I speak of the five aggregates in the world; one should have no attachment to the world.
By not being greedily attached to the world, one does not abandon the dharmas of the world."
The Bodhisattva can comprehend this, understanding that the world is naturally so;
seeing that the aggregates (skandhas) have no fundamental basis, they do not cling to worldly dharmas.
Whether there is gain or loss, whether there is praise or slander, [they remain equanimous].
Whether having a name or being nameless, they feel shame for the worldly dharmas of suffering and pleasure.
By means of great wisdom, though they move within the worldly dharmas, they do not see that which the world covets; their resolve for the Way is unshakable.
Gaining profit does not bring him joy; being cast aside, he does not grieve.
Firmly established like Mount Sumeru, no one can shake him.
Whether praised or reviled, his will remains ever equanimous.
Regarding names as nameless, and regarding suffering and pleasure with equanimity;
firmly abiding in a mind of equality, one understands that the world is natural and arises from inversion.
Not being born into the world, one proceeds alone in clear realization.
If one enters into the mundane world, thoroughly understanding the places one reaches,
then by following worldly customs, one delivers sentient beings from suffering;
though wandering in the world with vigor, one remains amidst the secular like a lotus flower.
Without destroying the conventional, one discerns the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Even if one acts within the world, one does not discriminate among worldly dharmas;
thus, while roaming amidst them, one thoroughly investigates the characteristics of the conventional.
The characteristics of the world are like space, and yet even in space there is no characteristic of emptiness;
having been able to understand this, one does not cling to the mundane.
According to what is known by the various worldly conventions, one transforms sentient beings in accordance with them.
Thoroughly penetrating the natural state of the world, one does not bring about its destruction or ruin.
If the five aggregates did not exist, this would be called the natural state of the world;
those who do not understand it always rely upon worldly conventions.
If one can relinquish all aggregates (*skandha*) and not give rise to the notion of non-existence,
though appearing in the world, one remains unattached to worldly things.
Those who do not understand the nature of worldly phenomena will burn with the fires of contention.
This is empty and false, devoid of sincerity; it constantly establishes itself in two characteristics.
I have never participated in the world, nor have I engaged in any dispute.
For this reason, the Buddha has categorized the natural Dharma.
The Dharma is without contention; it is that which all Buddhas have taught.
It thoroughly penetrates the equality of the world; it is not empty, but is ultimate sincerity.
Even if double-tongued speech were true, one would still fail to attain the Teacher’s command.
If one were to cause harm, it would be no different from the non-Buddhists.
As for those who truly examine all phenomena, there is neither reality nor falsehood;
therefore, the World-Honored One taught that there is no second dharma for transcending the world.
The worldly wisdom I have attained is the conventional law of the mundane world;
it is neither empty nor substantial, yet it reveals the evils of the world.
It serves as a light for the world and leads to the attainment of great renown.
The Buddha has opened and enlightened the world, Pure and free from all blemish.
If there are those who contemplate the conventional, And perceive the body as the spontaneous nature,
Then they shall behold the Samyaksaṃbuddha Manifesting throughout the ten directions.
Knowing that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, and that no phenomenon exists inherently,
one who analyzes these causes and conditions will be able to master the principles of the Dharma.
One who can thus understand and penetrate the Dharma will be able to clearly comprehend emptiness.
If one can understand and realize emptiness, one can distinguish the True Guide.
If one discriminates and discourses upon the world while seeking after sounds and voices,
though one performs worldly affairs, one does not dwell together with the world.
If one falls into various views, none can compare to this:
though using provisional names to wander in the world, one does not cling to worldly affairs.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who delight in patience—
While that Buddha is present, the Dharma-body of the Guide—
if one upholds such a teaching as this, one thereby makes an offering to the Buddha;
dwelling in the world as a World-Honored One, one is known by the Guide.
Even if the evil Māra Pāpīyān were to appear,
he could find no opportunity against one who dwells among humans and extensively expounds this sutra.
Such a person possesses great wisdom and is the master of bestowing all things.
Perfecting the observance of precepts, they understand the Buddha, the Teacher.
Possessing the courageous power of patience, they stride with diligence;
wise and attaining joy in meditative concentration, they discern the world.
"The Buddha speaks of emptiness and the non-existence of dharmas;
those who hear this are of such a class that before long, these Great Beings will dwell at the site of enlightenment and subdue the Māras.
Chapter Four: Explaining All Dharmas (1). The Buddha again addressed the Brahmā Mind-Holding:

"The Tathāgata has already transcended the realm of the world; yet he displays worldly teachings and practices to delight in the mundane, desiring to deliver those who find pleasure in the world by means of the cessation of that very mundane pleasure—this is what is called the five aggregates of the world."
He thinks to himself:
"The world is what I shall deliver; I shall bring the world to total extinction.
To seek within the five aggregates while wandering the path is called the "path of dualistic longing."
"Furthermore, Brahmā! Why is it called the five aggregates (pañca-skandha)? These five aggregates are merely conventional worldly designations;
because one seeks out all views, one abandons the acceptance of worldly conventions. That which is seen is but a natural conceptualization, and this is what is termed 'cessation' (nirodha)."
When one attains the path leading to cessation and does not accept any views, one thereby turns away from worldly desire toward the right path.
Therefore, Brahmā, the Buddha spoke these words:
"In the world there are three thorns and three heavy burdens; one should practice in the world, cease from the world, and exhaust the world in order to seek liberation."
Thereupon, the Brahmā Citta addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“If the Tathāgata were to speak of the matter of the Four Truths, to what do these truths ultimately resort?
The Buddha told the Brahmā:
"These are the truth of suffering and the truth of its origin; these are not noble truths. These are the truth of cessation and the truth of the path leading thereto;
these are not noble truths. Why is this so?"
If all forms of suffering were the Noble Truths, then all cattle, horses, mules, donkeys, dogs, pigs, and the various classes of animals would have attained the Noble Truths.
If all formations were the Noble Truths, then all beings born within the five destinies would likewise attain the Noble Truths.

If the exhaustion of suffering were taken as the Noble Truth, then all sentient beings, upon perceiving the phenomenon of annihilation, would immediately eliminate [all afflictions] and attain the Noble Truth.
Furthermore, by means of the Truth of the Path, all conditioned phenomena would result in the attainment of the path of the noble ones and the power of the Noble Truth.

For this reason, Brahmā! One contemplates suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as the Noble Truths; one who thoroughly understands that suffering does not arise—this is called the Noble Truth.
The practice of those people is not the Noble Truth; rather, that which is the dharma of cessation—neither arising nor ceasing—is called the Noble Truth.
If all dharmas are equal and there is no duality regarding the path, this is the Noble Truth of the Sages.
The Buddha told Brahmā:
"That which is called 'truth' (satya) is that which contains no falsehood.
What is meant by falsehood?"
To reckon for oneself that there is a body, to conceive of a person, to assume the existence of a life-span, and to speak of destiny;

to be attached to male and female, to rely on the three realms of existence, to be alienated from what truly exists, to depend on what arises, to rely on what ceases, to undergo birth and death, and to take refuge in nirvāṇa—this is called emptiness (or vanity).
Regarding all these sensations, among all sensations, there is no dependence and no seeking; this is called the Truth. To say "one who would eliminate suffering" is empty;
to say "the cessation of the origin of suffering" is also empty; to say "I shall fully realize it" is also empty; even the path of practice is likewise empty.
"Why is this so? The Eightfold Path taught by the Buddha, as well as the Four Foundations of Mindfulness—these too are called empty.
He asked again:
"What is that which is taught by the Buddha and what one should contemplate?
He replied: "To be without intention and without thought; all dharmas are likewise so. This is what is called that which is taught by the Buddha and what one should contemplate."

To practice the four foundations of mindfulness is to have no dwelling place; it is not to abide in any perceptions. One who does not abide in any perceptions dwells in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Having dwelt in the limit of reality, there is no dwelling and the mind has no locus.
If the mind has a locus, that is unreal and is called "emptiness."
For this reason, one should form this contemplation: that which is neither real nor unreal constitutes the Noble Truth.
That which is examined is the truth; and what is called "truth" is that which is neither produced nor can be made true.

Although the Tathāgata appears, he does not arise from anything; the Tathāgata does not abide in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) nor in nirvāṇa, and there is neither birth-and-death nor any fixed, permanent certainty.
"Why is this? Because these Noble Truths have neither birth-and-death nor nirvana.
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! If one realizes these four truths in accordance with the proper sequence, they are called the ‘Right Truths.
The Buddha told Brahmā:

"In a future age, there will be bhikṣus who cannot guard their bodies, do not protect the prohibitions and precepts, cannot restrain their minds, and are not refined in wisdom; yet they shall preach and expound, giving rise to the Truth of Suffering while claiming it leads to the Truth of Origination. Racing about in this manner, they destroy the various places of birth within the three realms of existence. Furthermore, they say that one should seek to practice the path; this is called racing about in the practice of the two truths."

These people are foolish and deluded; I designate them as the companions and followers of heterodox teachings. They are not disciples of the Buddha, nor are they my śrāvakas; their aspirations follow deviant paths, they destroy the true Dharma, and they are self-indulgent.

When I dwelt at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, there was neither a turning toward ultimate truth nor any falsehood; as for the Buddha, there is likewise no movement toward any phenomena.
For this reason, in seeking the Dharma of the Tathāgata, do not contemplate dualities, and do not speak of duality, for to do so constitutes a dualistic inquiry.
He replied, "I dare not, O God among Gods!"
He replied: "This is the path of inversion and delusion; it cannot eliminate all that one pursues.
Thereupon, Dharmacittin addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The Dharma of the Tathāgata is free from inversion and is likewise unattainable. Why is this so?
When the Tathāgata attained Buddhahood, he was given the title ‘Samyaksaṃbuddha’ (Perfectly Awakened One); what does this term signify?”
He replied: "According to what you perceive in the mind of Brahmā,
is the Dharma taught by the Buddha existent or non-existent?"
"Is it real or is it false? He replied,
"It is false, O God among Gods!"
"There is nothing that exists; one dwells securely in the ultimate sanctity.
He then asked the Brahmā:
"Does this dharma of emptiness have a place where it dwells, or does it dwell nowhere?"
He replied: "O World-Honored One!
That which is empty and non-existent neither abides anywhere, nor does it not abide."
He asked again: "How is it,
Brahmā, that regarding all dharmas there is neither abiding nor non-abiding?"
The Great Sage replied,
"In what way does one attain the Way? He answered:
"He has not attained the Path. He said, "Brahmā!"

The Tathāgata sat beneath a tree at the site of enlightenment; having fully understood that the objects of desire and the states of perversion are fundamentally and eternally pure, empty, and spontaneous by nature.
That which is fully understood is as if there were nothing to be understood, yet it is not that there is no understanding. Why is this?

For this reason, the Dharma I have understood and attained through perfect awakening is without seeing and without hearing, without thought and without cognition, without sensation and without attachment, and without any destination. It transcends all natures; it is without speech, without expression, without characters, and without phrases, nor is there any verbal instruction.
"In this way, Brahmā! All dharmas are like space; yet do you wish to attain all dharmas? He replied:
"No, O God among Gods! Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
The Buddhas, the Great Sages, are utterly beyond compare; they have attained the unprecedented and are fully endowed with the Dharma of truth.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess supreme great compassion; they discern and clearly understand the quiescent Dharma and explain it for others using words and letters. Those sentient beings who have faith and joy in the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma, establishing the roots of all virtues and fulfilling what is required—such beings incur no fault before the Buddhas.
Why is this? Because all in the world believe in him, and his mind is free from attachment.
Furthermore, O God among Gods!
The people of the world believe in the Dharma, regarding the Dharma as "mine," relying on the mundane and becoming attached to it.

The Dharma is neither real nor unreal; there is neither Dharma nor non-Dharma. Yet worldly people rely upon Nirvāṇa; when one examines this, there is neither beginning nor end, nor is there any Nirvāṇa. Worldly people rely on wholesome virtue, yet there is neither wholesome virtue nor unwholesome. Worldly people rely on peace and happiness, yet there is neither suffering nor happiness. Worldly people rely on the arising of a Buddha, yet the Buddha is neither born nor does he pass into parinirvāṇa.

"Furthermore, when preaching the Dharma, one should discerningly extol the Noble Assembly; taking the unconditioned as the basis for such discernment, that scripture shall be worthy of trust in the world."
"It is, for example, like using a metaphor where fire arises from water and water arises from fire; in all cases, it is due to the convergence of causes and conditions.
The Buddha said, "In this same way, awakening to and understanding sensory desires is the very cause and condition by which one attains the Buddha-way."

Why is this so? It is because that by which the Tathāgata awakened to and understood the afflictions (*kleśa*) and attained perfect enlightenment is itself no attainment of perfect enlightenment. Although there is that which is taught, he does not perceive form; nor does he have any thoughts, nor does he construct duality, nor does he have anything to realize. He does not attain *nirvāṇa*, nor is there any quiescence.
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who understand and believe in this Dharma, they will be able to eliminate all views and attain liberation; they should prostrate themselves, take refuge, and pay homage to them as if to the Tathāgata.”

Regarding the Buddhas of the past, he has already performed practices for them and thus constitutes a virtuous friend; he is protected by what he perceives, his aspiration is sublime, he has planted the roots of all virtues, and he has already attained the treasury of tranquility and truth.

To grasp the treasury of the Dharma is to extinguish all transgressions; to establish the path of practice is to attain noble birth; to uphold the essence of the Tathāgata’s teachings is to be a great giver; to cast off worldly defilements is the power of guarding the precepts; to be free from the power of craving and desire is the power of patience; to be boundless in the vigor of angerlessness is the power of diligence, being without weariness or sloth; to be the power of meditative concentration is to abandon and eliminate sinful karma; and to be the power of wisdom is to relinquish false views. Thus, no demons whatsoever can cause one to waver, and no enemies or adversaries can achieve victory over them.

He never deceives or deludes those in the world; his words are most sincere, and his expositions are clear and thorough. That all phenomena are fundamentally pure is the truth; that he preaches the ultimate Dharma is the protection of the Tathāgata. He delights in benevolence and harmony; his dwelling is peaceful and secure, which constitutes true wealth. Regarding the work of the noble ones, he knows contentment; regarding the conduct of the noble ones, he clearly perceives their cultivation. Through diligent service, he shall be seen and trusted as one who has crossed to the other shore; for those whose will is liberation, he provides encouragement.

To those who delight in liberation, he enables their prompt deliverance; to those without refuge, he provides a place of reliance. To those who delight in non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), he leads them to attain *nirvāṇa*; to those who delight in the Path, he provides a broad exposition. To those who aspire to transcendence, he manifests his presence; furthermore, regarding various arts and techniques, he acts as a King of Physicians, providing excellent medicine for all who are ill. To bring them to wisdom, he serves as a supportive ally; once they have attained spiritual power (*anubhāva*), they find joy in attaining sovereign mastery, neither depending on others nor receiving instruction from them, remaining free from fear so that their hair does not stand on end.

"Like a lion’s stride, he attains the sublime vehicle; like a divine dragon, his mind is peaceful and harmonious; like a tamed elephant, he moves among the multitude; like a celestial immortal, he achieves valor; having subdued his enemies, he traverses the great assembly with a firm will, free from fear, his purpose fulfilled, and acting with self-mastery and intrepidity."

The True Realities thus expounded are entirely free from difficulty; they eliminate the dharma of worldly toil like the full moon, and their light of wisdom shines afar like a torch. Like the rising sun, there is nothing it does not illuminate; it extinguishes all darkness like a burning lamp. Free from all attachments, it neither increases nor decreases; its sustaining practice is like the earth, upon which all sentient beings rely for their livelihood.

"He is like a fertile field where the hundred grains flourish; he washes away all defilements like water; he extinguishes all conceptualizations like fire; he is unattached to any phenomena like the wind; he is immovable like Mount Sumeru; his will and nature are as firm and strong as a diamond or the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), such that no heterodox practitioners can withstand him, and no Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can equal him."

Because the equal flavor of the Dharma is like the great ocean, he is a teacher who delivers others; he eliminates the thirst of all worldly afflictions and, in his yearning for the sutras and the Dharma, never feels satiated. Thus, his wisdom is never overfull, and as a holy sovereign, he turns the wheel of the Dharma.

"His countenance is exceptionally beautiful, like that of Śakra, Lord of the Devas; his mind attains mastery, like that of Brahmā; he proclaims the Dharma with a thunderous roar, like the gathering of celestial clouds; and he rains down nectar, like a torrential downpour upon a vast marsh. Thus, one gains long-term increase in the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment; one attains transcendence over the afflictions of birth and death; one enters into the noble wisdom of the Buddha; one draws near to and reaches the true path of the Buddha; one shall obtain extensive learning without peer, surpassing all measure and being truly immeasurable; one’s wisdom and eloquence will have no equal; one attains *dhāraṇī* and possesses a firm and resolute nature; and with an intellect that is penetrating and brilliant, one perceives the dispositions of all living beings."

"Contemplating all phenomena, his resolve was fully realized; he constantly practiced loving-kindness and compassion for the people of the world. Having already attained transcendence over worldly affairs, his conduct was unattached like a lotus flower, untainted by mundane dharmas, and thus beloved and revered by all the wise."
Those of great learning mostly follow him; he is constantly respected and obeyed by the multitude of wise men.
All devas and worldlings serve him, and the assembly of those in meditative concentration bows their heads in salutation to him. The assembly of worthy sages all comes to honor and attend upon him;
he is held in common esteem and praise by both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and thus he delights in seclusion from the land.
In their conduct, they are free from flattery and artifice, do not covet gain or offerings, and possess a majestic and towering spiritual power as they tread the path of the sages and saints.
Their appearance is upright, extraordinary, and elegant, such that their countenance is difficult to equal; their radiant splendor is so brilliant it cannot be fully described or fathomed.
Thus, they adorn themselves with the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha, are able to uphold the teachings of the Buddha, and are able to follow them accordingly.
They shall protect the teachings and scriptures of all dharmas and also be able to assist and deliver the assembly of sages and saints;
they shall constantly attain the vision of all Buddhas and Perfectly Awakened Ones, and by this means, they shall swiftly perfect the eye of the Buddhas.
When they are seen by the Buddhas and receive their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), they shall then attain the fulfillment of the three kinds of patience (*kṣānti*).

Soon you shall attain your seat beneath the Bodhi tree, where you will be able to subdue Māra and his retinue, obtain all supernatural powers and wisdom, and turn the wheel of Dharma; thus you will be able to initiate and perform the various deeds of a Buddha, proceeding toward the profound Dharma without fear, without dread, without difficulty, and without anxiety.
“O Heaven among Heavens!

Even if I were to spend an eon, or even more than an eon, extolling and proclaiming these true beings, I could not reach the limit of their supreme virtues or the extent of their practice. The Way of the Buddhas is as profound and subtle as this; it is difficult to receive, difficult to understand, difficult to behold, difficult to comprehend, and difficult to realize.”

If there are those who receive and uphold it, recite and read it, and further practice it according to its teachings; and if they can extensively expound and widely distribute it, then regarding that Dharma teaching, they will be able to establish the foremost profound faith among the assembly.
The Buddha told Brahmā:
“As for the virtues of the true sages that you have praised, how could one ever exhaustively fathom them?
One cannot know them as fully as the Buddha has fathomed them.”
The Tathāgata, by means of unimpeded wisdom, fully expounds his virtues; only then can one thoroughly understand and exhaustively realize them.

Regarding the meaning and intent of the phrases spoken by the Tathāgata, all these true persons shall fully comprehend them; they shall universally accord with them without opposition or disorder, acting with utmost sincerity rather than confusion. They shall establish correct discourse with minds that do not wander, and regarding matters of adornment, they shall understand them through appropriate expressions. This is like the verbal teachings expounded by the Tathāgata, or as when the Great Sage preaches the Dharma of ultimate truth, or again, like the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata which transcends such adorned phrases. Being unable to exhaustively fathom or fully awaken to all things, they are neither following nor opposing, neither constrained nor liberated; only then do they attain true knowledge and remain free from negligence regarding adornment, no longer relying on what is known through mere words.

Even if there were no words, this would still be the speech with which the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma; it is through the sūtras that the Tathāgata expounds that he skillfully proclaims the Dharma. The Tathāgata, moved by the arousal of infinite compassion, unfolds and sets forth these scriptures for the sake of sentient beings.
The Buddha told Brahmā:

"If a bodhisattva can discern and understand the causes for which the Tathāgata’s five powers provide healing, such a one is a bodhisattva who is then able to establish and perform the various deeds of a Buddha."
He asked the World-Honored One again:
"What are the five powers by which the Tathāgata provides healing?
The Great Sage replied:

It means that one enters into the verbal expressions of the Dharma as they should be taught; through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one illuminates the Dharma without losing its phrasing or meaning, and by discerning the tracks of the Path, one enters into great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
The Buddha said,
“Brahmā! This is what is healed by the five powers of a Tathāgata, which no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can equal.”
He asked the World-Honored One again:
"With what words does the Tathāgata expound the teaching?
The World-Honored One replied:

“O Brahmā! The teachings of the past, future, and present; discourses on sensual desires and inverted speech; worldly and world-transcending matters; the outflowing and the non-outflowing; attachment and non-attachment; the blameworthy and the blameless; existence and non-existence; and all expressions concerning the self, person, life-span, and the realization of attainment, as well as expressions concerning the cycle of birth and death and nirvana—these, O Brahmā, are [the dharmas].”
Regarding all these various expressions that are spoken: one contemplates expressions as being like illusions, because they are not established;
