one contemplates expressions as being like dreams, because what is seen has no reality; one contemplates expressions as being like echoes, because they are responses to sounds arising from conditions; one contemplates expressions as being like shadows, because they exist through the convergence of conditions; one contemplates expressions as being like reflections in a mirror, because they appear through illumination; one contemplates expressions as being like forms produced by seals, because they exist through impression; one contemplates expressions as being like flames, because they are seen through inversion; one contemplates expressions as being like space, because their existence is exhausted; and one contemplates expressions as being beyond speech, because they cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha said to the Brahmā:
"If a bodhisattva can thoroughly understand the verbal expressions of all these dharmas, that bodhisattva is then able to expound upon the verbal expressions of all dharmas."

Furthermore, they have no dependence upon any phenomena; because they have no dependence, they are able to attain unimpeded eloquence (*anāvaraṇa-pratibhāna*). Because they have attained unimpeded eloquence, they can manifest the radiance of equality for all obstructed beings, and while dwelling together with them, they preach the Dharma without obstruction. Regarding all words and phrases, they do not destroy the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); they traverse all speech and even that which is refuted, remaining entirely without dependence.
"Furthermore, Brahmā! That which the Tathāgata speaks is the manifestation of the ineffable; this is what constitutes preaching the Dharma. Brahmā!"
If you wish to know which bodhisattvas perform acts of truth toward the Tathāgata and exercise skillful means therein, O Brahmā!
The Tathāgata manifests afflictions within the sensory objects (*dhūta*) and manifests the sensory objects within afflictions; a bodhisattva should fully understand this course.
"What do you mean, Brahmā? [he asked].
How does the Tathāgata manifest afflictions (*kleśa*) within the dust of the world?

Because the dust of worldly toil is naturally equal and without distinction. Furthermore, he manifests worldly toil within affliction; relying upon affliction, he practices giving and attains the purity of *nirvāṇa*. This is because all the foolish and ignorant are unable to comprehend the suffering inherent in these various afflictions.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva clearly understands that all matters of giving are great treasures for future lives, and thus has no destination.
That which has no destination is called the unconditioned precepts and nirvana; for they are entirely non-existent and involve no activity.

Patience is unconditioned because it is empty and non-existent; diligence is unconditioned because it follows the cultivation of the mind; meditative concentration is unconditioned because there is nothing to be delighted in; and wisdom is unconditioned because it attains the marks [of reality].

Regarding the original limit of desire and the absence of desire: it is because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is without desire. Regarding the original limit of hatred: it is because one reckons that within the nature of phenomena there is no resentment or enmity. Regarding the original limit of delusion: it is because one reckons that within the nature of phenomena there is no delusion. Regarding the original limit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nature of birth and death: there is nothing that arises therein. That which is unconditioned does not rely upon birth and death. As for the words and speech regarding what is seen as either ultimate sincerity or falsehood—where falsehood is taken as ultimate sincerity, this leads to arrogance and self-indulgence.
"Furthermore, Brahmā!

The Tathāgata follows the sequence of the True Truths and, according to their causes and conditions, reckons that there is permanence. Knowing that there is a self serves to eliminate improper matters; for those with false views who lack firm faith, he creates counter-karmic actions to make them understand the consequences of their reversals, thereby removing their lack of faith and completely eliminating their desires."
The Tathāgata fully knows those with wrong views and accordingly explains them for their sake; to those who should see [the truth], the Tathāgata then teaches the instruction of ultimate reality.
If sentient beings were to abandon their arrogance and conceit, the Tathāgata would then teach and expound for them with his own truthful and authentic instruction.
This, Brahmā, is what it means.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has taught this instruction; therein, the Bodhisattva should thoroughly understand these skillful means.
If one takes refuge in all these explained provisional skillful means, then upon the arising of the Tathāgata, one shall attain liberation.

Those who have firm faith in that which is not a wrong matter perceive the retributions manifested in various forms and thereby give rise to [the thought of] sentient beings; thus, through the Tathāgata, they attain liberation.

If one expounds the Dharma-body, it constitutes the Tathāgata’s words of ultimate truth; one practices firm faith by liberating oneself from false dharmas and, through the Dharma, delivers those who revere mere letters. This is not taught to the various classes of sentient beings, for they do not understand the dharma that resolves false views and have never believed in this; thus, there is neither attainment nor distinction.
To speak of there being nirvāṇa is to hold false faith;

to abide amidst the inversions and afflictions without striving for or attaining extinction—this is true faith through which one attains liberation, wherein the non-arising of dharmas does not destroy any phenomena.

To speak of "a person" constitutes false belief; for one who enters into stillness and seeks to deliver others, there is no such person. For that which is falsely believed is itself the matter of liberation through the True Dharma.

"Therefore, Brahmā! Regarding these bodhisattvas, those who cannot fully comprehend the skillful means of their words concerning ultimate truth will find no fear in any sound as they guide and benefit immeasurable numbers of people and classes of sentient beings."

In this regard, Brahmā! By what skillful means does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, preach the Dharma for sentient beings? Those who practice giving attain great wealth; those who maintain the precepts are reborn in heaven;

those who practice patience become upright; those who exert diligence obtain clarity; those who practice meditative concentration achieve joy and non-distraction; those who study wisdom eliminate the defilements and attachments of craving; those who are extensively learned swiftly attain wisdom; by practicing the ten wholesome deeds, one attains residence in the heavens or among humans; by practicing loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, one ascends to the Brahma-heaven; by observing tranquility and serenity, one obtains the fruits and reaches the stage of learning (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*); one attains the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*) and the stage of the Pratyekabuddha; and through the pure blessings of the Buddhas, one attains the stage of the Buddha-way. The wisdom thus manifested is boundless, equal to Nirvāṇa, and extinguishes all suffering.
The Buddha said, “Brahmā!

It is by means of timely and skillful expedient means that I proclaim and reveal such a Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; yet the Tathāgata has never harbored various conceptualizations in his mind, nor has he reckoned in terms of self, person, or life-span.”

The conduct of the Tathāgata is likewise without anything to be attained; he is neither stingy nor greedy, yet there is nothing given in charity; he neither observes precepts nor violates prohibitions; he is neither patient nor wrathful; he is neither diligent nor indolent; he is neither in meditative concentration nor distracted in mind; he is neither wise nor foolish; there is neither a path nor is there extinction; there is neither peace nor is there any affliction.
The Buddha said, “Brahmā!

To teach and transform sentient beings so that they may practice with diligence, devotion, and fulfillment—by reason of such diligent, devoted, and fulfilling practice, they shall enter this Dharma according to their original vows. Some may attain the fruit of the Path: the stage of Stream-enterer, Once-returner, Non-returner, or Arhat, up to the level of Pratyekabuddha; or again, they may enter and achieve the unsurpassed, right, and true path, reaching the liberation of the unconditioned. This, Brahmā, is what it means.”
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, through his skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), expounds the sūtras for the sake of sentient beings.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva should likewise employ skillful means for the sake of sentient beings, giving rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and constantly encouraging and rescuing them by means of the true Dharma.
What is it that the Tathāgata has taught?
It is that phenomena have no eyes and there is no liberation; the ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise without liberation.
Why is this so? The eye is empty;

there is no "I" and no "mine," and it is thus fundamentally pure. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise: they are empty, and because there is no "I" and no "mine," they are all fundamentally pure.

The Buddha said, “Brahmā! This is the gate of liberation to which all things ultimately return. To have a destination toward which one tends is to be deluded; it is the same for the six objects—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena. All dharmas are entirely empty: they are without perception, without aspiration, without arising, and without cessation; they neither abide nor do they not abide. That which is called ‘mind’ does not abide in birth; it is fundamentally pure, naturally tranquil, and utterly still.”
The Buddha said: “Brahmā!

The Tathāgata expresses everything through written characters as gates of liberation. Whether by means of phrases that govern delusion or folly, he universally accords with written characters; one should contemplate them in the mind as the teaching of ultimate truth. Everything that the Tathāgata can distinguish leads to liberation, and whatever can be spoken is entirely a phrase of truthful reality.”

The Tathāgata has taught that in the sūtras there is no defilement; all the dharmas he expounds are without liberation or entry into nirvāṇa. This is the scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, and this is what a bodhisattva should study.
The Buddha addressed Brahmā:
“By what skillful means does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, fully cultivate great compassion and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?”
The Tathāgata employs thirty-two matters to dispatch [beings], and through great compassion, delivers sentient beings.
What are these thirty-two? There is no self;

regarding all dharmas, he causes the various classes of sentient beings to understand and believe in the absence of a body—this is the first instance where the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
First, although all phenomena are devoid of a sentient being who experiences them, beings nevertheless conceive of such a person; regarding them, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Second, all phenomena are devoid of a life-principle (*jīva*), yet beings falsely reckon that there is a life-principle; regarding them, the Tathāgata manifests great compassion.
Third, all phenomena are devoid of a lifespan (*āyus*), yet beings falsely reckon that there is a lifespan; regarding them, the Tathāgata manifests great compassion. Fourth...
5. All dharmas are non-existent, yet sentient beings conversely calculate them to have a location; thus, the Tathāgata arouses great compassion for them. 6.
All dharmas are entirely without dependence, yet sentient beings conversely rely upon and cling to them.
7. All dharmas are entirely void and non-substantial, yet sentient beings conversely set their minds on what they find pleasant.
8. All dharmas are entirely devoid of a self, yet sentient beings conversely reckon that there is a self;
9. All dharmas are entirely without a master, yet sentient beings conversely fix their minds on greedily grasping and receiving them;
10. All dharmas are entirely without anything to be received, yet sentient beings conversely rely upon and depend on physical forms and appearances.
11. All dharmas are entirely without arising, yet sentient beings conversely cling to that which arises;
12. All dharmas are entirely without cessation, yet sentient beings conversely crave birth and death;
13. All dharmas are entirely free from the dust of desire, yet sentient beings conversely sink and drown in defilement.
14. All dharmas are entirely free from desire, yet sentient beings are instead defiled by it;
15. All dharmas are entirely free from anger, yet sentient beings instead harbor resentment and hatred;
16. All dharmas are entirely free from delusion, yet sentient beings are instead bewildered by them.
17. All dharmas come from nowhere, yet sentient beings conversely delight in relying on their destinations;
18. All dharmas go nowhere, yet sentient beings conversely rely upon beginnings and endings;
19. All dharmas are devoid of volitional activity, yet sentient beings conversely strive to establish what they cultivate.
Twenty: All dharmas are entirely free from negligence, yet sentient beings instead gallop about in unrestrained indulgence;
Twenty-one: All dharmas are entirely empty and still, yet sentient beings instead dwell upon what they perceive;
Twenty-two: All dharmas are entirely without conceptualization, yet sentient beings instead regard conceptual activity as supreme.
23. All dharmas are entirely without aspiration, yet sentient beings instead direct their will toward what they crave;

having already distanced themselves from various kinds of things, as for that which is received—namely, the worldly reliance on anger and resentment—it results in affliction and weariness, such that one does not congregate with enemies, nor dwell in impatience, but rather abides in benevolence and harmony.

24. Following inverted views is what is practiced by the world and wandering upon deviant paths; one is thus able to cast off the places where [such views] arise. 25. [The text continues: ...and so forth.

They lack discernment regarding the path to be followed; they become agitated by the pursuit of wealth and profit, which are the dependencies of the secular world, and they set their hearts upon all manner of material resources. One should therefore restrain these insatiable desires so as to be fully endowed with the treasures of the noble ones—faith, precepts, shame, dread of blame, learning, generosity, and wisdom—and thus establish oneself in these seven treasures.

(26) I say that sentient beings are slaves to affection and craving; they take what is not firm or essential to be firm and essential. Wealth, occupations, home, and the pleasures of wife and children bring no true peace. This is why they are called slaves to affection and craving: among the classes of sentient beings, there is nothing firm or essential, yet they conceive the notion of solidity. For their sake, one should preach the reckoning of the impermanent for those who reckon things as permanent, and manifest the truth of impermanence. (27)

28. I say that when sentient beings seek wealth and profit, it constitutes enmity and resentment, yet they conversely regard such pursuits as being for their true kin and friends; I therefore establish for them the practice of manifesting true kinship and friendship, thereby eliminating the afflictions of toil and suffering and ultimately leading them to *nirvāṇa*.

29. I say that because sentient beings engage in perverse karma, each remains mired in various verbal teachings; I shall therefore preach for them the pure, subtle, and sublime life free from karma, expounding the Dharma through analytical distinctions. 30.

I say that sentient beings are defiled by the dust and grime of the world, and that within the affairs of household life there are many harms, calamities, and distractions; I shall therefore preach the Dharma to cause them to depart and transcend the three realms.

31. When sentient beings dwell amidst all conditioned phenomena, abiding in the signs established by the various conditions arising from greed, and become indolent and negligent in their practice therein, [the Tathāgata] shall preach the Dharma for the sake of the noble liberation, exhorting them to diligence as the essential means of deliverance, and expounding the sūtras so that they may all attain peace; furthermore, he surpasses them by bestowing the unimpeded wisdom. 32.

When those who seek the most honored nirvāṇa set their minds upon the inferior states of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, [the Tathāgata] shall manifest for them the subtle and wondrous conduct; it is for this reason that the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward sentient beings.
The Buddha told Brahmā:
"These are the thirty-two matters by which the Tathāgata guides, transforms, and accords with sentient beings, spreading and propagating great compassion;
this is what is called the Tathāgata practicing great compassion."
The Buddha told Brahmā:

"If there is a bodhisattva who practices these thirty-two matters and gathers great compassion (mahākaruṇā), such a bodhisattva, being a mahāsattva, is called a great field of merit and possesses great majestic power. Delighting in the sublime, they reach the stage of non-retrogression and establish their practice for the sake of all sentient beings."

When the Buddha spoke this chapter on the Dharma-gate of Great Compassion, thirty-two thousand people resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Chapter Five: On Difficult Questions (2).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"When the Brahmā Cittadhara heard the Tathāgata’s discourse on great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he was neither joyful nor sorrowful regarding the dharmas thus analyzed."
Cittadhara replied:

"If a son of good family practices the two modes of knowledge, that person will experience both joy and sorrow. However, in the state of the true limit (bhūtakoṭi), these two things are forever absent; for this reason, one neither rejoices nor grieves."
It is like the marvelous illusions performed by a magician, and like the actions of those conjured figures who reach a state of neither joy nor sorrow.

This son of good family has already attained entry into the spontaneous nature of all phenomena; he spontaneously beholds the transformations manifested by the Tathāgata, experiencing neither joy nor sorrow.
Those emanated by the Tathāgata, upon hearing the eloquence spoken by the Tathāgata, feel neither joy nor sorrow.

Even if they thus discern all phenomena as being entirely like illusions, without distinction, they do not feel intense delight toward the Tathāgata, nor do they harbor thoughts of inferiority toward sentient beings.
Jālinīprabha asked again:
"Virtuous one, have you already understood that all dharmas are illusory in nature? He replied:
“O son of good family!
If there were practices regarding all phenomena and a locus for them, one might indeed ask such a question.
He then asked the Brahmā:
"What is it that you, O Benevolent One, practice? He replied,
"That which all foolish commoners follow and practice is precisely where my own practice lies."
He asked again:
“Fools practice lust, anger, delusion, and doubt; they reckon the body to be their own physical frame and consider it ‘mine. They dwell in wrong views. Why, O Venerable One, do you dwell among them?”
He replied: "Do you wish to cause ordinary persons to reach the state where they have accomplished the dharma of being no longer ordinary? He answered:
"I do not wish to delight in the affairs of ordinary worldlings; how then could I set my mind upon the accomplishment of dharmas?

Son of good family, it is like this: all dharmas are without accomplishment; dharmas have no place of abiding and no place of accumulation; they are without resentment and without forgetfulness, nor is there any harboring of retribution."
He replied: "Noble son!

To be free from lust, anger, and delusion, and not to engage in any phenomena—this is called 'characteristic. That which involves engagement is the practice of ordinary worldlings, whereas this is the practice of the noble ones. Where there is engagement, two things arise."
Furthermore, son of good family!
All practices are non-practice; all teachings are non-teaching; all abodes are non-abiding; and all destinations are non-destination.
He asked the Brahmā again:
"What is meant by 'all actions being non-action'? He replied:
"Even if one were to practice the teachings for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, one would not know any increase or decrease in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
For this reason, all that is practiced is non-practice."
He further asked the Brahmā:
"What is meant by 'all that is taught being without anything taught,' and 'all that is a place of abiding being without any place of abiding'?"
He replied: “All dharmas are that which the Tathāgata has taught and that in which the Tathāgata abides.
For this reason, all that is taught is non-teaching, and all that is abided in is non-abiding.”
He asked again:
"What is meant by saying that all destinations are non-destinations? He replied:
“There is, in truth, no person who goes to any place of rebirth; for this reason, all places of going are actually places of no-going.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Dhṛtimat, saying: “Excellent!”
"Excellent!
If you wish to speak, you should deliver this discourse.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha asked the Bodhisattva Cittadhara:
"As you have just described to me, noble sir, all that is practiced by foolish commoners is precisely where my own practice lies.
If this is so, does it mean that one who practices in such a manner will attain some gain?"
He replied: "How could one's wandering be restricted by the place where one is born, such that it would limit what one can practice?
He then asked the Brahmā:
"If one does not manifest through birth, how can one teach and transform sentient beings?
He replied, "Just as the Tathāgata manifests through transformation-birth, so do I manifest."
He asked again:
"Does that which is emanated by the Tathāgata have birth? He replied:
"Is there anything that should be manifested through transformation?
By whom is the realm of the Buddha brought forth? He replied:
“There is that which manifests and that which is manifested, as well as their objective spheres; yet although there is manifestation, it is a non-manifestation.
He replied: “I should cultivate this contemplation regarding what is produced: that which is produced is established through the conditions of the realms.”
He asked again:
"Virtuous one, do you perhaps practice the cycle of birth and death through causes and conditions? He replied:
"I have no causal conditions for the practice of birth and death.
He asked again:
"For this reason, by what causal conditions does one encounter objects and experience fear?"
He replied: "Just as with causes and conditions, so too is the fear regarding the realm of causes and conditions; for one who reckons that there is no fundamental basis, there is no retrogression.
Thereupon, the elder Śāriputra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O God among Gods! If there were someone who, together with these various devas and nāgas, entered into discourse, they would obtain immeasurable merit. Why is this so?
"Now, World-Honored One!
It is most wonderful that we have been able to hear the names of these true beings;
how much more so, then, to encounter them as they preach the Dharma!"
It is like a tree that grows and stands upon the earth, yet manifests its trunk, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits in the open sky.

In this same way, O Great Sage, one should regard the conduct of these true beings (*satpuruṣa*): they abide in all phenomena while manifesting birth, death, existence, and disappearance; they circulate and travel through, manifesting within all Buddha-lands, having attained mastery by means of such supreme and wondrous wisdom and unimpeded eloquence.
"Having seen such transformations of wisdom as these, what son or daughter of good family would not resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment?
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Samantakusuma who said to Śāriputra:
"Venerable sir, have you not entered into this nature of phenomena (dharmatā)?"
“The Buddha has said that among the elders, you are the most venerable in wisdom; why then are you unable to be moved by such a transformation?
He replied, “The World-Honored One has declared me to be foremost among the śrāvakas regarding the knowledge of their respective spheres.”
He asked again:
"Can the assembly explain the realm of the Dharma? They replied:
"No," he replied.
He asked again:
"How is it, Elder, that you have something to expound according to your own realm?"
He replied, “As it is that which has been entered, so too is what has been spoken.
He asked again:
“Venerable sir, can one bring about the realization that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is boundless? He replied, “It is so.”
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'whatever one enters into, what one speaks is likewise so'? O Śāriputra!"

According to the limitations of what one enters, the limitations of what one explains are likewise; thus, to impose such limits is to bind the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) itself, yet that nature of phenomena has no boundaries.
He asked Puhua again:
"Does that dharmatā have no characteristic of entering? He replied:

"O Śāriputra! Even if the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has no characteristic of entering, and within the nature of phenomena there is no characteristic of that which enters, for what reason do you so earnestly apply yourself to the nature of phenomena with the intent of liberation?"
He replied, “No. He asked again:
"If it is so regarding equality, it is likewise for the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as it enters into accordance with suchness. He replied: "Puhua!..."
"I myself wish to see it and also wish to hear it.
He replied, "Indeed, Śāriputra!"
"How can the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) have anything to be contemplated?
Do all phenomena have anything that is spoken or heard? He replied:
"No. He asked again: "Virtuous one, for what reason do you say that there is something to be seen and something to be heard?"
He replied: "Puhua! The World-Honored One has said:..."
"There are two kinds of people who obtain immeasurable merit:
those who single-mindedly and diligently preach the Dharma, and those who listen with a focused mind.
For this reason, O Benevolent One, you should expound the Dharma, and I shall listen to it.
The Brahmā asked again:
"Venerable sir, can one who has extinguished all conceptual thought still contemplate in meditative concentration and listen to the Dharma? He replied:
“Son of good family!
For one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation, there is no principle by which they could hear the Dharma through two things. He replied:
“Venerable Śāriputra! Is your mind at ease?
Are you tranquil regarding fundamental purity and all phenomena?”
He replied: "It is so, son of good family!
All dharmas are fundamentally pure and quiescent."
He replied: "Therefore,
Venerable Śāriputra, you are not capable of constantly remaining in meditative concentration while listening to the Dharma."
"Why is this? Because all dharmas are fundamentally and entirely quiescent. Śāriputra asked:
“Noble son! Are you able to preach the Dharma without arising from meditative concentration? He replied:
"Indeed, Śāriputra! Can one apprehend any phenomena through examination?
Yet you, sir, say that it is not by arising from meditative concentration that one is able to preach the Dharma?"
He replied, "It is not so. Brahmā spoke again:
"Therefore, O virtuous one, all the ranks of ordinary, foolish, and ignorant people constantly attain a concentrated mind.
The elder spoke again:
"By what concentration do ordinary, foolish, and ignorant people enter samādhi?"
He replied, "That all dharmas have no destination— this is called 'constant concentration' (nitya-samādhi).
He asked again:
"Is there, then, no difference between such practitioners who are ordinary, foolish, and ignorant,
and those who are noble and holy? He replied, "Indeed, Śāriputra!"
It is exactly as you have said. Furthermore, what I observe is that I do not wish to create any distinction between ordinary, foolish people and the noble sages. Why is this so?
The dharmas of the noble ones are not extinguished, nor do the dharmas of the foolish and ignorant arise; they are equal to the dharma-realm. For this reason, there is no one who crosses over.
He then asked again:
"Son of good family!
What is meant by 'all dharmas are without origin'?"
He replied: "If one acts according to what the elder’s body discriminates and knows, how could one further give rise to the dharmas of the noble ones? He replied:
"No," he replied.
He asked again,
"Does your benevolence consist in the eradication of the dharmas of ordinary persons?"
He replied, "No. He asked again:
"Could one ever attain the dharmas of the noble ones? He replied, "No!"
He asked again:
"Do you still further differentiate the dharmas of ordinary persons? He replied:
"Not so. He asked again, "How does the Elder discern and know the proper time?"

He replied: "The Dharma as it has been heard is free from the state of ordinary beings and thus is without basis; equality is likewise without liberation, and nirvana is likewise without basis and likewise suchness."
He replied: "O Śāriputra!
That which is without origin has no differentiation and is not manifold; that which is without origin has no destination."
"What is called 'having no root'—as with that which has no root, all dharmas likewise enter into having no root.
Thereupon, the Elder Śāriputra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Heaven among Heavens!"

Just as a great fire, blazing and radiant, burns everything without exception, so too it is with these sons of noble family: they discern and understand all the teachings they proclaim, leaving no aspect of the nature of all phenomena unexhausted.
The World-Honored One said:
"Indeed, Śāriputra! It is as you have said;
the sons of good family expound the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) in this very manner."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha said to Śāriputra:
"The Buddha has praised your wisdom as supreme!
When he praises you, Venerable One, by what wisdom does he do so?"

He replied: "Jālinīprabha, you should know that among the śrāvakas, those who rely on sound merely illuminate their own bodies to attain liberation; it is only in reference to them that I am praised as the most honored. It is not because I possess wisdom superior to that of the bodhisattvas."
He asked again:
"O Śāriputra! When you examine wisdom, do you perceive any characteristic of speech?"
He replied, “It is not so. He asked again:
"Is the practice of that wise one not universal?
Is it not impartial? He replied:
"It is so; it is exactly as you have said: wisdom is equal.
He asked again, "For what reason is the universal equality of all phenomena called wisdom, yet you instead speak of the limitations of wisdom?"
He replied: "Indeed, son of good family!
The Dharma-nature of wisdom has no boundaries or limits; those who are bound by limits follow their own spheres of experience, entering it through the practice of fundamental wisdom."
He asked again:
"That which you know is infinite; can it be limited? He replied:
"Not so. He asked again: "By what limit do you bind yourself so as to have something to say?"
At that time, Śāriputra remained silent and spoke no word.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, receiving the holy intent of the Buddha, stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!”
"For what reason is the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha called 'Jālinīprabha'?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, seeing that the elder Mahākāśyapa had made this request and wishing to cause the assembly to become fully endowed with the roots of virtue, addressed Jālinīprabha:
"O son of good family!"

Having manifested the pure radiance resulting from the karma created by one's own original virtues, one shall display brilliant splendor for the sake of those in the heavens and the people of the world, so that the bodhisattvas whose roots of goodness and resolve have matured may either give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment or attain diligent progress.

Upon hearing the Buddha’s summons, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha adjusted his robes and, from the webbed fingers and nails of his right hand, emitted rays of light that penetrated immeasurable and incalculable distances, illuminating the boundless lands of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions and pervading all infinite and innumerable Buddha-worlds.

Those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; the multitudes of sentient beings who are blind, deaf, mute, or speech-impaired; those with lameness, physical infirmity, or disease; those who are emaciated, insane, deluded, or ignorant; those harboring lust, anger, and folly; those who are naked and uncovered; those who are hungry or thirsty; those who are imprisoned or bound; those who are impoverished, ugly, aged, decrepit, or at the point where death is their due law; those who are stingy, greedy, jealous, or envious; those who violate the precepts, harbor malice, are indolent, or licentious; those with evil wisdom, lacking faith and extensive learning, and ignorant of shame and remorse; those fallen into the sixty-two false views and doubts; and those born in the eight difficult states where there is no leisure—all these receive this light and immediately find peace.
At that time, those sentient beings were free from lustful desire, suffered no anger, and were not deluded by ignorance; they harbored no resentment and experienced no burning affliction.

At that moment, before the World-Honored One, the entire assembly of those who had gathered—bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—all appeared as a single form, entirely golden in color. They all manifested equally, with physical features and appearances identical to those of the Tathāgata, universally manifesting the single mark of the invisible crown of the head.

Their bodies were like adamant; they all sat upon naturally arisen lotus flowers beneath jeweled canopies with interlacing pendants and parasols of various gems, all of which were equal and without distinction.
They manifested natural bodies no different from those of a Buddha; all embodied beings attained peace and security, just as Bodhisattvas who have attained samādhi each give rise to joy.

At that time, the assembly marveled at what had never occurred before; as they looked at one another, everyone appeared exactly like the World-Honored One without any distinction, and no longer perceived their own bodies as flawed.
As soon as this light was emitted, four bodhisattvas from the lower direction suddenly leaped forth and stood with palms joined, each thinking to himself:
"To which Tathāgata should we now pay homage?"
A voice from the air then spoke to him, saying:
"The extraordinary radiance of the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha causes the entire assembly to appear as a single color, manifesting in the likeness of the Tathāgata."
At that time, the four bodhisattvas attained what they had never experienced before, and raising their voices, they said:

"If that which we have established through our utmost sincerity is true, then let the forms and colors we now behold be of one kind without difference; let all dharmas be equal and without distinction."
Since this truth is not false, we shall specifically behold the miraculous manifestation of the Buddha Śākyamuni; if we see the Tathāgata, we shall serve him with devotion.
At that time, the World-Honored One’s lion throne, adorned with interlaced lotuses, rose seven feet above the ground.
Then the four bodhisattvas prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and spoke in unison:
“It is truly unprecedented, O God among Gods!”
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible.

Such are the virtues and vows of the Bodhisattva Mingwang (Net of Light), whose fundamental nature is pure; he emanates such radiance that the majestic countenances manifested by all sentient beings appear in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha:
"O son of noble family!

Withdraw the vast radiance manifested by your light; having performed the work of a Buddha and established much benefit, you have caused immeasurable people to set their minds upon the path of enlightenment."
Upon hearing the Buddha’s command, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha withdrew his light.
Instantly, the entire assembly returned to its former state, and their dignified deportment and ritual etiquette reappeared as they had been before.
The Tathāgata was seated alone upon the lion throne, when the elder Mahākāśyapa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From where have these four bodhisattvas come?"
The four bodhisattvas replied,
"We have come from a different buddha-field in the lower direction.
He asked again:
"What is the name of this world?
He replied, "Universal Manifestation of All Jewels."
He asked again:
"What is the name of the Tathāgata, the Arhat?
Is he currently preaching the Dharma?"
He replied, “His name is Ekaratnacchattra Tathāgata, and he is preaching the Dharma there.
He asked again:
"How far is that world from here? He replied,
"World-Honored One, you know this."
He asked again,
"For what reason have you venerable ones come here? They replied:

“The Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha radiates light; I saw that light from my own land reaching down to the Buddha-land below, and there I heard the name of the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni, and of the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha. Therefore, I have come to this land desiring to behold the World-Honored One, to prostrate and serve him, and to see the noble being, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha.”
Then Mahākāśyapa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One, how far is the world-system Sarvaratnapratibhāsa, the buddha-field of the Buddha Ekaratnacchattra?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Seventy-two Ganges-river-sands of Buddha-lands below this world, one reaches the world called Universal Manifestation of All Jewels, the abode of the Buddha Single Jewel Canopy; it is from there that these four bodhisattvas have come."
He asked the World-Honored One again:
"How long did it take to reach here?
The Buddha replied:
"In the mere instant of a single thought, he has already arrived here.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"How inconceivable is the Great Sage!"
The light emitted by these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas and their sublime, majestic spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) are thus.

As the Bodhisattva Mingwang (Net of Light) radiates his brilliance, illuminating the far reaches without limit, these four Bodhisattvas have now arrived here. Who, upon seeing such transformations of spiritual power and the deeds wrought by wisdom, would not aspire to and take delight in establishing the Mahāyāna?
The World-Honored One said:
"As you have stated, the practices of the bodhisattvas are inconceivable and cannot be matched by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
6. Chapter on Questions and Discourse (2). Chapter Six: Questions and Discourse. Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha:

"Noble son, your radiance is like that of the Tathāgata; your majestic presence and countenance are of the hue of purple-polished gold, and the assembly, receiving this brilliance, appears as if all were of uniform appearance."
He replied: "O Mahākāśyapa!
You should question the World-Honored One so that he may provide an answer. Thereupon, the Elder immediately stepped forward and questioned the Great Sage.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"When the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha attains Buddhahood, all those in his assembly shall possess countenances of purple-gold, and they will all delight in the single principle. With one mind and firm faith, they shall attain all supernatural penetrations and wisdoms; there shall be no names of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but only a multitude of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
“If there are bodhisattvas born in that buddha-field, should they not be called Tathāgatas?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Thus it is, Kāśyapa! As you have said, one may indeed be called a Tathāgata.
At that time, forty-four thousand people all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, vowing to be reborn in that land; with one voice and in unison, they all exclaimed:
"When the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha attains the Way of the Buddha, we shall all be born in that Buddha-land.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After how many *kalpas* will Jālinīprabha attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and become a Most Rightly Enlightened One?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Ask Mañjughoṣa-Jālinīprabha himself how long it has been since he attained Buddhahood; he shall explain it for you.
Then the elder Kāśyapa asked Mañjughoṣa-Jālinīprabha:
“O son of noble family!
How long will it be before you shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment as the Most Perfectly Awakened One? He replied:
“Kāśyapa, suppose someone were to ask:
‘How long will it take for a person created by a magician to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment as the most perfectly awakened one?’”
"How would you answer him? He replied, "Noble son!
"What could a magician’s creation, being empty and without reality, possibly answer? He replied:
"In this way, all phenomena are like magical illusions, spontaneously formed; why ask such a question?"
"O Benevolent One, how long will it be before you attain the most perfect enlightenment?
He asked again:
"What do you mean, son of good family?"

It is just like that which is conjured by a magician; the illusion is tranquil and cannot be distinguished, being without conceptualization and without words. Do you mean, O Benevolent One, that all phenomena are likewise?
"By what means and through what stages do you benefit and guide sentient beings? He replied:

"As the Way is spontaneous (*svabhāva*), so too is the person spontaneous; as the person is spontaneous, so too is illusion (*māyā*) spontaneous; as illusion is spontaneous, so too are sentient beings spontaneous; and as sentient beings are spontaneous, so too are all phenomena (*dharmas*) spontaneous."

O Mahākāśyapa! Calculating it in this way, one should not regard it as being beneficial or non-beneficial, nor as being neither beneficial nor non-beneficial; there is neither crossing over nor not crossing over.
He asked again:
"Do you not establish sentient beings in the Buddha-way? He replied:
“Does the path of the Tathāgata involve the formation of mental conceptions? He replied, “No!”
For this reason, I do not establish the various classes of sentient beings in the Buddha-way, nor do I cause them to aspire to the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
O son of good family!
"Now, O Benevolent One, upon what do you stand? He replied,
"Just as there is no foundation upon which to stand, that upon which I stand is likewise so."
He asked again:
"If there is no fundamental basis, then there is nothing established, nor is there any returning. He replied:
"In this way, it is like that which has no root and nothing upon which to stand, and likewise no retreat.
That which is rootless is also like this: it stands where there is nothing to stand upon."
"For this reason, I say that all dharmas neither arise nor recede.
He then asked Mingwang:
"O Benevolent One!"
"For what reason do you transform and enlighten sentient beings, yet say that there is neither establishment nor regression? He replied:

"If one possesses understanding and penetration, and has set their will upon a vow for subtle and wondrous matters, they do not transform sentient beings; furthermore, regarding all dharmas, those who regress are likewise not transformed."
He asked again:
"O son of noble family! Do you not cause sentient beings who have not yet returned [to the cycle] to transcend birth and death?"
He replied: "I do not even attain the matter of birth and death, nor do I have anything to see; how much less could I return to sentient beings?
He asked again:
“Virtuous one, have you not been transformed through the succession of births and deaths among the ranks of sentient beings until reaching Nirvāṇa?
He replied, “I have not attained Nirvāṇa, nor have I seen anything.”
For what reason do you exhort and transform the various classes of sentient beings?

For example, son of good family, if there were no beginning or end and no attainment of parinirvāṇa, for what reason now do you exhort, transform, and guide countless people to practice the Buddha-way?
"Do these sentient beings not seek liberation? He replied:
"If a bodhisattva were to attain birth-and-death, there would be nirvāṇa."

"It is because of the conceptualization of sentient beings that one says there are people who practice the Buddha-way; yet they cannot be called Bodhisattvas, nor should it be said that they are seeking the Buddha-way.
He asked again:
"O son of noble family!..."
"In what sphere do you practice?
He replied, "In my own practice, I do not practice within birth and death, nor do I practice within nirvana; I have no perception of sentient beings."
"O Mahākāśyapa! As for what you asked just now regarding where one practices:
that which is the practice of an emanated Tathāgata is precisely the practice from which my own practice also proceeds."
He replied: "Son of good family!
An emanated Tathāgata does not engage in any activity."
He replied: "The characteristics of all sentient beings are likewise; one should not observe them while engaging in practice.
He asked again:
“Noble son! Do you observe the conduct of sentient beings in this way?
For what reason do sentient beings engage in lust, anger, and delusion?”

“Since that manifested Tathāgata is undefiled, free from fetters and resentment, and without forgetfulness, I shall now question you, Venerable One; please answer as you see fit according to what you know.”
"Furthermore, Venerable One, do you perhaps possess this lust, anger, and delusion? He replied, "Not so."
He asked again:
"Are lust, anger, and delusion truly exhausted? He replied:
"Not so. "If an elder were without lust, anger, and delusion, yet did not extinguish them, where would that lust, anger, and delusion be transferred? He replied:
"O son of noble family!

Foolish ordinary people dwell in perversion; their thoughts and mental constructions involve longing and seeking—whether appropriate or inappropriate—and they thus habitually practice lust, anger, and delusion."

Furthermore, the noble sages, through the Dharma and Vinaya, awaken to and realize the nature of perversity; they no longer practice or cultivate discursive thoughts and mental formations, and being free from both the appropriate and the inappropriate, they are thereafter devoid of lust, anger, and delusion.
"Kāśyapa, what do you think? Since all phenomena arise from perversion, do they proceed from a cause?
Do they have an origin?"
"Is it because they are unarisen? He replied, "Noble son!"
"Since there is no arising, there is nothing that arises.
He replied: "Indeed so, Mahākāśyapa!"
“What is your intention?
Since that which has no arising and nothingness does not exist, how could there be anything that arises? He replied:
"Not so," he replied. "It is thus, O Mahākāśyapa!"
"If that which has not arisen is to be made to arise, where would it arise? He replied, "It is not so."
He asked again:
"Venerable sir, do you give rise to lust, anger, and delusion by seeking that which is born? He replied:
"Not so," he replied. "For this reason, O Mahākāśyapa!"
"From what do lust, anger, and delusion arise?
Is it because sentient beings cling to attachments that they bring about worldly toil? He replied:
"It is so, it is so, son of good family!
All dharmas are fundamentally and entirely pure, being free from lust, anger, and delusion. He replied:
"For this reason, I have said that all dharmas are entirely like illusions and transformations; such is the natural mark of the Tathāgata.
When these words were spoken, forty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience that accords with the Dharma (anulomikī-dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti).
Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Whoever beholds Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha with their own eyes shall not fall into the evil destinies, and the hosts of Māras shall be unable to find an opportunity against them."
If there are those who hear this Dharma being preached, these bodhisattvas will never fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
as for those who see and receive instruction upon what is taught, the Buddha has already praised the virtues of the land of the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: “Kāśyapa,
wherever the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha travels through Buddha-fields, he transforms, edifies, and liberates countless sentient beings.”
“Do you see those sons of noble family who have been graced by this light? He replied, “I see them.”
The World-Honored One replied:
"Suppose the three thousandfold great thousandfold world system were filled with mustard seeds; their number could be known and their quantity distinguished.
Yet the number of people whom the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha has converted and established upon the Buddha-way is immeasurable."
Kāśyapa! If you wish to know of the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, even if sentient beings see his radiance, he will preach the Dharma through skillful means.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Listen to what I say: this son of noble family’s buddha-field is exceptionally distinguished, named the Realm of the Pure and Radiant Net of Light (*Vimalaprabhājālin*).

After six hundred and seventy million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed, the Bodhisattva Jālin will attain buddhahood, known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, named Universal Radiance Sovereign King of Shifting Light (*Samantaprabhā-vikampita-raśmi-rāja*).
The world is named Equal Assembly of Excellence;
as soon as one approaches the Bodhi tree, one attains Buddhahood.
In that Buddha-land, there are no Māras or Māra-devas, and all beings are resolved upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
That Buddha-land has exquisite sandalwood as its soil; the world is level and even like the palm of a hand or like the webbing between a bird's toes.

The bodies of the sentient beings in that realm are supple and soft; the land is harmonious, gentle, peaceful, and fertile. The entire Buddha-land is composed of all manner of precious jewels; it is free from the impurities of sand, gravel, stones, and thorns, and there is no suffering or affliction of the evil realms. Furthermore, there is no severity of the eight difficulties or lack of leisure.
"In that Buddha-field, lotus flowers grow everywhere; these lotus flowers are all made of jewels, and they are exceedingly fragrant and come in various colors.
The world is vast and expansive, its extent in the east, west, south, and north being beyond measure."

The Tathāgata King of Universal Radiance and Shifting Light has an immeasurable multitude of bodhisattvas who follow his voice; through the majestic spiritual transformations of the Buddha-dharma and the noble assembly, they have already attained adornment by light and reached the treasury of dhāraṇīs. Possessing unimpeded eloquence, wisdom, fame, and virtue, they have acquired great supernormal powers to subdue all māras. Their minds always dwell in a sense of shame, and they cultivate holy brilliance with diligence, transforming others through wisdom.
The Buddha said: “Kāśyapa!
Furthermore, in that buddha-field, no women are born; all bodhisattvas are born from precious lotus flowers and grow naturally to maturity.”
These bodhisattvas take dhyāna as their food; their dwellings, places for walking meditation, couches, bedding, palaces, bathing pools, gardens, pavilions, and estates are like those in the heavens.

The Tathāgata King of Universal Radiance and Shifting Light preaches the Dharma of the sutras without the use of written words; rather, when the bodhisattvas are illuminated by the Buddha’s radiance upon their bodies, they immediately attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This light exhausts and dries up the defilements of lust, anger, and ignorance. Furthermore, other rays of light reach the realms of other Buddhas, extinguishing the dust of form and desire among sentient beings so that they are left without blemish; these beings thus accord with the discipline.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Within that radiance, the sounds of the Dharma-gates naturally emerge, manifesting thirty-two matters.
What are these thirty-two?"
All phenomena are empty, for they purify all views;
all phenomena are signless, for they are free from conceptualization;
all phenomena are wishless, for they transcend the triple world.
All dharmas are free from desire, for they are fundamentally pure and tranquil;
all dharmas are free from anger, for they eliminate all conceptualizations;
all dharmas are free from delusion, for they transcend all darkness.
All dharmas have no coming, for they do not arise at all;
all dharmas have a future, for they accord with contemplative observation;
all dharmas have no abiding, for they are established spontaneously.
All dharmas are eternally transcended, for they have no past, future, or present;
all dharmas are without distinction, for they are spontaneous (*svabhāva*);
all dharmas are without arising, for they are without retribution.
All dharmas are without the retribution of creation, for they do not arise;
all dharmas are without action, for they arise from conditioned conduct;
all dharmas are without form, for they exist through dependent recollection.
All dharmas are formless, being detached from all that is born;
all dharmas are profoundly true, awakening to the reality;
all dharmas are most sincere, being of one and the same equality.
All phenomena are devoid of a person, for there is no person to be found;
all phenomena are devoid of a life-principle, for they are the ultimate reality;
all phenomena are devoid of a sentient being, for they do not receive instruction.
All dharmas are protective and watchful, for they eliminate all fetters;
all dharmas are without attachment, for they are free from feverish affliction;
all dharmas are without proximity, for they are fundamentally pure and free from dust.
All dharmas are of one essence, for the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is tranquil;
all dharmas are serene, for they constitute a single samādhi;
all dharmas abide in their original source, arising only in response to conditions.
All dharmas are without fundamental activity, yet they are subject to the destruction of conditions;
all dharmas are the dharma of universal equanimity, universally entering into all things;
all dharmas are without conditions, for they do not intermingle or become confused.
"All dharmas are awakening, for they accord with how they appear;
all dharmas are unconditioned, for there is no engagement with manifold phenomena.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:

"This is the radiance of the Tathāgata Samantaprabha-cala-prabhārāja; from it issues forth such sounds. By means of this radiance, he performs the work of a Buddha for the sake of bodhisattvas, and in that buddha-field there are no demonic activities nor any hindrances or obstructions."
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa,
"Furthermore, the lifespan of that Tathāgata is immeasurable.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"If there should be anyone who wishes to take up the Buddha-land, they must receive the pure realm of a Buddha in this very manner; now, son of good family, you shall immediately become fully endowed with all things in universal completeness."
The Buddha said,
"As you have stated, from the presence of incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Tathāgatas, your vows have been purified.
At that time, the Brahmā Dharaṇīdhara addressed the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha:
“Does the Tathāgata now grant the prediction of enlightenment to this son of good family? He replied, “Brahmā!”
"The Tathāgata bestows predictions of enlightenment upon all people.
He asked again:
"In what manner does he bestow these predictions?"
He replied, "To receive retribution in accordance with what one has done— this constitutes receiving a prediction.
He asked again:
"For what reason is the prediction of retribution bestowed?
Why is the prediction granted to you, O Venerable One? He replied:
“Brahmā! As for what is called ‘conditionality,’ the body performs no action, the mouth utters no speech, and the mind cannot be perceived; can this be considered the creation of demerit or merit?”
He replied, "Not so. He asked again:
“Does that Buddha-way have any characteristics of practice? He replied, “Not so.”
"The Way has no form and possesses nothing; the Way is nameless and devoid of the characteristics of activity.
He asked again:
"If there is no activity, how can one cause the Way to have the appearance of activity and thereby achieve attainment?"
He replied, "It is not so. "Therefore, Brahmā! [he said.]
One should speak thus: if there is no creation, there is no retribution; if there is neither the appearance of practice nor the nature of practicing, this is called the Way.
Just as with the Way, so it is with the recipient; it is like receiving the prediction [of enlightenment], yet it is also like receiving the prediction without the appearance of practice.
He asked again:
"Noble son! Is it that one receives the prediction [of enlightenment] only after not practicing the six perfections?"
He replied: "It is so, Brahmā!
One must practice the six pāramitās before receiving the prediction of enlightenment."
Furthermore, when the noble sages relinquish all defilements, this is called the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā);
when they practice nothing and create nothing, this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā);
when there is nothing they cannot endure, this is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
If one is serene and detached, this is called the Perfection of Vigor;
if one dwells according to what is appropriate, this is called the Perfection of Tranquility;
and if one fully understands all things, this is called the Perfection of Wisdom.
"Furthermore, Brahmā!
If there were a bodhisattva who practiced these six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā), would there be any [inherent] action? He replied:
“There is no practice. Why is this?

If there were one who practiced as they should, and if there were something to be practiced, then that which is practiced would be non-practice; it is only when there is nothing to be practiced that this constitutes true practice.”
He replied: "Therefore, Brahmā, you should establish this teaching:
that which is without practice is itself the practice of the Way."
Furthermore, Brahmā spoke thus:
"Have you already received the prediction of your attainment of the Way?

If the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally non-existent, then that which is seen as receiving the prediction by this non-existence is such that my own reception of the prediction is likewise so."
He replied: "Son of good family!
That which is without basis and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) are both entirely without the bestowal of prediction."
He replied, “The signs of receiving the prediction of enlightenment are likewise so; they are just like the absence of a fundamental basis and the equality of dharmas, without any distinction.
Thereupon, the Brahma-deva Dharmacintin addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“What is the practice of that bodhisattva by which they receive the prediction of enlightenment and attain the unsurpassed, perfect, true path?
The Buddha told Brahmā:
“If a bodhisattva’s practice is such that they do not give rise to practice, nor do they extinguish it, and they do not engage in practice...”
There is neither good nor evil; one neither conforms to worldly conduct nor transcends the world. There is neither sinful action nor meritorious action;
there is neither transgression of conduct nor non-transgression. There is neither outflowing action nor non-outflowing action;
there is neither the performance of action nor the non-performance of action. One neither engages in action nor is detached from action.
There is no practice of non-dedication, yet no departure from dedication; there is no practice of eradication, yet no non-eradication;
there is no practice of birth-and-death, yet no nirvana; there is no practice of seeing, yet nothing heard; there is no practice of mental intention, yet nothing known;
and while not practicing giving, there is no stinginess or greed, and while not upholding the holy life (brahmacarya), there is no [transgression].
Regarding what is transgressed, there is neither the practice of patience nor the lack of patience; neither the practice of vigor nor indolence;
no practice of meditative concentration and no single-pointed focus; no practice of wisdom nor lack of wisdom;
and neither the practice of penetration nor any entry.
The Buddha told Brahmā:
"If a bodhisattva practices in this manner, the Tathāgata shall grant him this prediction that he will attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
Why is this? O Brahmā! If one were to practice according to what is appropriate, there would be something practiced and a will directed toward some creation.
If one practices the Path while giving rise to conceptual formations, or practices the Path without conceptual formations; whether there is purposeful action or no purposeful action;
and whether one practices the Path with negligence or without negligence, or with playfulness or without playfulness—if such is the practice of the Path, it is not the true practice of the Path.

For this reason, Brahmā, you should know that you must not hold such a view; when one has transcended all conditioned activities, one is then a bodhisattva who receives the prediction of enlightenment.
Again, he asked: "Indeed, World-Honored One!
What is meant by 'receiving a prediction' and 'attaining a prediction'?"
The World-Honored One replied:

"To eliminate all duality regarding all dharmas is called receiving the prediction; to not construct duality regarding all dharmas is called receiving the prediction; to regard all that arises as equal to various forms is called receiving the prediction; and for one's body, speech, and mind to be tranquil is called receiving the prediction."
The Buddha told Brahmā:

"I recall that in a past age, there was an eon named Priyadarśana. During that eon, I made offerings to seventy-two koṭis of Tathāgatas, yet none of those Tathāgatas bestowed upon me a prediction of enlightenment."

Furthermore, there was an eon named Good Transformation (*Suvyūha*); during that eon, he made additional offerings to twenty-two billion Tathāgatas and others, yet he did not receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Furthermore, there was an eon named Brahmastava; during that eon, I again made offerings to eighteen thousand Buddhas, yet I did not receive the prediction of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there was an eon named Prīti; during that eon, I further made offerings to three million two hundred thousand Tathāgatas, but those Tathāgatas likewise did not grant me the prediction.

After that, furthermore, there was an eon named Mahāvyūha; during that eon as well, eight million four hundred thousand Tathāgatas appeared, all of whom I made offerings to, serving them with various kinds of things according to their needs, yet those Buddhas did not grant me the prediction of enlightenment.
The Buddha told Brahmā:

“Suppose now, for an eon or even more than an eon, I were to speak the names of all the Tathāgatas, the number of Buddhas I have made offerings to in the past, and furthermore, my dwelling there to cultivate pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), offering every gift and article of worship without exception, observing all precepts to their full completion, upholding patience and loving-kindness while remaining free from fetters and resentment, practicing diligent vigor, comprehending and retaining everything heard, maintaining a single-minded concentration where one’s conduct is tranquil and one sits in focused reflection, and even possessing the wisdom of speech through inquiry—yet none of these Tathāgatas granted me the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).”
Why is this? It is because one relies upon conditioned formations. "Brahmā!..."
If you wish to know this, you should cultivate this contemplation: one must transcend all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); this is called the Bodhisattva receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
Thereafter, upon encountering the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, one will then attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Dīpaṃkara, the Perfectly Awakened One, saw him and conferred upon him this prediction, saying:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha, named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat."
At that time, he transcended all practices and was fully endowed with the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā). Why is this?
Because he had completely relinquished all conceptualizations (saṃjñā), this is called the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).
To eliminate all causal conditions wherever they arise is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*);
to endure all natures is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);
and for all conditioned activities to be entirely quiescent is called the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
To have no habitual practice regarding any thought is called the perfection of tranquility (śamatha-pāramitā);
to realize original purity and give rise to the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
Upon seeing Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, I immediately became fully endowed with the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).

Since I first resolved my mind [on enlightenment], everything I have relinquished and bestowed—whether it be a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, or a hundred-billionfold—cannot be compared to, nor can it serve as a metaphor for, the merit of offering the five lotus flowers. It is beyond all comparison.

"From the first resolution, they practiced giving with contentment, observed prohibitions and conformed to the precepts, and through patience, gentleness, and harmony, they ultimately accepted humiliation and remained steadfast in the Dharma. With diligent and earnest application, they cultivated practice without weariness; through meditative concentration, they remained in profound stillness, always free from attachment. From the first resolution, they contemplated wisdom and were never negligent. When one calculates this wisdom against the various *pāramitās*, it is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, and even a trillionfold greater—beyond comparison and beyond metaphor."
"Therefore, Brahmā! You should form this contemplation:
at that time in that world, he immediately fulfilled the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
He then asked the World-Honored One:
“How does one fulfill the six perfections?
The Great Sage replied:

“Not dwelling on giving, not clinging to precepts, not conceptualizing patience, not fixating on diligence, having no abiding place in meditation, and non-duality in wisdom—this is what it means to fulfill the six perfections.”
He asked again:
"If one is fully endowed with the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), what is it that is fully endowed? He replied:
"If one is fully endowed with the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), one is then immediately endowed with all supernormal knowledges and wisdom.
He further asked the World-Honored One:
"If one is endowed with the six perfections, how does one become immediately endowed with all supernormal knowledges and wisdom?"

He replied: "Brahmā! If one is equal in giving, then one is equal in all supernormal knowledges (abhijñā); if one is equal in ethical discipline, then one is equal in supernormal knowledges; if one is equal in patience, then one is equal in supernormal knowledges; if one is equal in diligence, then one is equal in supernormal knowledges; if one is equal in meditative concentration, then one is equal in supernormal knowledges; and if one is equal in wisdom, then one is equal in supernormal knowledges. By being able to equalize these, one equalizes all phenomena, and thus becomes equal toward all supernormal knowledges."
"Furthermore, Brahmā!

One who is fully mindful of giving is endowed with supernormal wisdom; one who is fully mindful of precepts, patience, diligence, tranquility, and wisdom is likewise endowed with all supernormal wisdom. To be free from thoughts regarding these supernormal wisdoms is called being fully endowed with the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and being complete in all supernormal wisdom."
"In this way, Brahmā!
Having been able to fulfill the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), one then fulfills the wisdom of the various supernormal powers (abhijñā).
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'possessing the wisdom of all supernormal powers'? The Great Sage replied: "The eye does not receive forms;

the ear does not receive sounds; the nose does not receive fragrances; the mouth does not receive flavors; the body does not receive tactile sensations; and the mind does not receive dharmas. There is nothing internal and nothing external; there is no point of departure, no reception, and no self-reflection. This is to be fully endowed with the pervasive and discerning wisdom of all supernormal powers."
Having fully perfected this, it is called "all-encompassing supernormal wisdom.
The eye does not cling to forms; the ear to sounds, the nose to fragrances, the tongue to tastes, the body to tangibles, and the mind to mental phenomena—there is no clinging whatsoever.

For this reason, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is unimpeded; what he perceives is limitless, and he attains all supernormal knowledges (abhijñā), yet he does not again grasp at those supernormal knowledges. Why is this so?

If one wishes to accomplish the vessel of all supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), then it is not accomplished as a vessel, for there is no vessel; being without a vessel is called "exposure. One who is able to practice this exposure with equanimity has nothing to receive regarding these supernormal knowledges.
It is just as, Brahmā!

All that is done depends entirely upon emptiness, yet emptiness has nothing upon which it depends. Everything is fully realized with nothing unknown, yet one aspires to and relies upon the wisdom of the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), while regarding those supernormal powers themselves as having nothing upon which to depend or seek.
He asked the World-Honored One again:
"What is meant by 'one possessed of all supernormal knowledges' (sarvābhijña)?
For what reason is one called 'one possessed of all supernormal knowledges'?"
The World-Honored One replied:
“Those who possess all-encompassing wisdom merely rely upon provisional names.

Being entirely without attachment and universally understanding all modes of practice, they have no concern for the matters of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; this is called ‘those who possess all-encompassing wisdom.’”
To investigate all thoughts and treat them accordingly is called the wisdom of universal penetration;
to discern all destinations to which beings go is called the wisdom of universal penetration;
and to know the conduct of sentient beings with limitless intelligence is called the wisdom of universal penetration.

To discern all things and accord with them at the appropriate times according to what has been learned, no longer training in the wisdom of the pratyekabuddhas, and manifesting teachings in response to the moment without anything being unpenetrated—this is called universal penetrating wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*).
To provide equal healing and act in accordance with beings without missing the proper time—this is called universal penetrating wisdom.
To clearly know which medicines can heal which ailments—this is called universal penetrating wisdom.
To eliminate all illnesses is called omniscience;
to uproot all obstructions and the fundamental sources of attachment is called omniscience;
to abide constantly in samādhi is called omniscience.
To have fully realized all dharmas without the net of doubt is called the wisdom of universal penetration;

to reach ultimate and universal understanding such that there is nothing unknown, and to expound the wisdom that liberates the world and transcends the world, is called the wisdom of universal penetration;

to exercise comprehensive mastery and discernment, such that one’s teachings are complete and all-encompassing with total agility and insight—O Brahmā! This is called the wisdom of universal penetration.
"Therefore, it is called 'all-pervading wisdom' (sarvābhijñā).
Thereupon, the Brahmā Citta addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"It is truly unprecedented, O God among Gods!"

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess no [discursive] mind; because of wisdom, it is called "mind," yet the mind is fundamentally pure. The Tathāgatas, the Truly Realized Ones, thoroughly and completely understand the mental activities of sentient beings.
"Certainly so, Great Sage!
If there were sons or daughters of good family who heard of these various forms of universal wisdom, who among them would not resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path?"
Thus, such immeasurable virtues are brought forth, giving rise to something truly extraordinary.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“If a bodhisattva aspires to the path while harboring expectations for fame and virtue, they do not truly yearn for the Buddha-way nor establish themselves in the Mahāyāna.”
Why is this? Because all dharmas are without name or merit, and have no faction or partisan.
O God among Gods!
This is not what constitutes the name and virtue of a bodhisattva.
O God among Gods!
When there is no longer any conditioned response, only then is one said to have established the will for the Buddha-way.

Because of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), desiring to extinguish the suffering, afflictions, and distress of sentient beings, they endure their own toil without weariness or fatigue, and do not fear the beginning or the end. Because it is immeasurable; because they do not sever the Buddha’s teaching; because they protect the True Dharma (*saddharma*); because they revere the Noble Assembly (*āryasaṃgha*); furthermore, because they eliminate unwholesome dharmas through wholesome dharmas; because they liberate and deliver them by means of the gates of liberation from all views; because they treat and eliminate all illnesses so that they are utterly extinguished; because they rescue and deliver all beings to birth in auspicious realms; because they lead and extricate those they love and hate; because they have no attachment to worldly dharmas; because they cause those pursued by the perilous path of birth and death to attain escape; and because they cause them to abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and strive for peace and security.
"O Heaven among Heavens!
Furthermore, all bodhisattvas should not harbor doubts or expectations; they should not act for the sake of sentient beings with any longing, nor should they have any uncertainty."
O God among Gods!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not become weary or disheartened by suffering or pleasure.
O God among Gods!
"What is meant by the purity of a bodhisattva’s lineage?
The World-Honored One replied:
"A bodhisattva does not rely on the lineage of a universal monarch (cakravartin), nor on that of Śakra or Brahmā; wherever they are born, their lineage is pure."
That a bodhisattva establishes the foundations for possessing all roots of virtue and inspires the source of manifold goodness in others constitutes the purity of a bodhisattva’s lineage.

Furthermore, when born among animals, they remain free from all [wrong] views; with loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and protective care, they impartially bestow the medicine of the Dharma to eliminate the defilements of the mind—this is the purity of a bodhisattva’s lineage.
Generosity is the lineage because it is free from stinginess;
ethical discipline is the lineage because it is free from the torment of remorse.
Patience is the spiritual lineage, because it is free from ill will;
diligence is the spiritual lineage, because it is without indolence;
meditative concentration is the spiritual lineage, because of one-pointed mental stability.
Wisdom is the lineage, for it is free from obscuration;

this constitutes the bodhisattva’s abandonment of all defilements without forsaking the aspiration for enlightenment, which is the lineage of a bodhisattva, because they take no pleasure in the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
7. Chapter on Discourse (2). Chapter Seven: On Discourse. Thereupon, the Brahma-deva Cittadhara addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The youth Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta sits here in this assembly in silence; he speaks no words and engages in no discourse.”
The Buddha said to Puśya:
"Can you take delight in dwelling here to preach this Dharma?
Is there any place where you must bend your will to provide an exposition?"
Viśeṣamati addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the dharma-principle by which one attains perfect enlightenment, does that dharma possess verbal teachings?”
He said, "Viśeṣacintin!
The Dharma is without verbal instruction."
He asked again:
"Does that Dharma have words and phrases, or does it involve thoughts and reflections, or can it be expounded and discussed? He replied:
“Dharmas are without words, without thought, and without discourse.
He asked again:
“If all dharmas are without words, without thought, and without discourse, then they cannot be taught.”
The Brahma-deva Cittadhara said to Pūrṇamukha, "Do you not,
O Benevolent One, expound the Dharma for the sake of other sentient beings? He replied:
"Brahmā! Can the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) be distinguished as two? He replied:
"Not so. He asked again: "Is that dharma-nature not something that can encompass all dharmas?"
