Chapter 8: On Tranquility (3). Chapter Eight: On Tranquility.
At that time, the Brahma-deva Dhāraṇīdhara addressed the Bodhisattva Samantagāmin, saying: “Noble son!
“Virtuous one, what kind of practice do you engage in?
He replied, “As for my practice, all conditioned phenomena are entirely non-existent; yet, I practice in accordance with the attachments of sentient beings.”
He asked again:
"Regarding all sentient beings who act out of attachment, what is meant by 'the conduct of sentient beings'? He replied:
"It is from the practice of all Tathāgatas.
He asked again:
"By what practice do you reckon that all Tathāgatas practice, such that it is considered their practice?"
He replied, "To practice with the realization that all things are eternally empty.
He asked again:
"Are all the practices of ignorant ordinary beings also the same as the practices of the Tathāgatas?
If that were so, what would be called the realm of the Tathāgata?"
He replied, "Do you wish to make a distinction between emptiness and existence? He answered:
"No," he replied. [The other] asked: "How so?"
“Does the World-Honored One not say that all phenomena are empty? He replied, “It is so.”
He replied: "For this reason, all dharmas are without distinction.
Furthermore, this practice is without marks."
“Brahmā, you should know that the Tathāgata does not dwell in various distinctions among all phenomena.
Thereupon, the Brahmā Dharmacittin asked Viśeṣamati:
“As for what is called ‘practice,’ what is the practice?”
He replied: "To practice the four Brahma-vihāras is what is meant by 'practicing.
He then asked the Brahmā again:

"One who practices the four brahma-vihāras does not wander in emptiness; wherever one performs practice, one constantly cultivates the four brahma-vihāras. Only when all such practices are fully perfected does one truly wander in emptiness."
"O Brahmā! Even if one dwells in seclusion or stays in the wilderness, if they are always fully endowed with the four brahma-vihāras, this is called 'wandering in emptiness.'"

Even if one were to dwell in lecture halls or pavilions, with purple-golden couches and seats arranged in layers, yet fail to practice the four Brahma-vihāras, this cannot be called "wandering in the void"; it is because one does not understand the conduct required for such a state.
He asked again:
"By what kind of conduct does one practice the conduct of wisdom-vision? He replied:
"If a practitioner is empty, they do not perceive a body.
He asked again:
"This non-perception of a self—is it the perception of wisdom?"
He replied: “It is so, Brahmā! One who does not see a self beholds wisdom.”
It is just as, Brahmā,
when there is a wise king, if his ministers and officials are sagacious and enlightened, they will possess wisdom and be held in high esteem by the sovereign.
"It is so, it is so; he who does not see me beholds pure wisdom.
He asked again: "Who does not see me?"
He replied: "The dharma of 'self' does not exist; those who possess such a category [of views] are fully endowed with a body. It is this kind of person who is called one who 'sees the self.'"
He asked again:
"According to the principle of what you have just said, I observe that one who does not see me is the one who sees the Buddha. Why is this so?"
"I and the Buddha are both naturally so. Pūrṇamukha!
What is it that the Tathāgata perceives?"
He replied: "One must be free from the view of a self. Why is this so? Because..."
"Not seeing me is to see the Dharma; he who sees the Dharma is one who sees the Buddha.
He then asked Puśya:
"If the conditions for non-self are fulfilled, does that lead to equality?"
He replied: "Brahmā!
Even if one were to accomplish all conditioned phenomena, could that truly be called attaining equanimity?"
He asked again: "How is this so, Puṣya?"
"By what means is one attained to and accomplished in equanimity? He replied:
"By neither discarding anything nor realizing anything; he who honors this attains equanimity."
He asked again:
"What does that wisdom-eye behold? He replied:
“Brahmā! That which is the eye of wisdom has nothing to see; that which is the eye of wisdom does not see the conditioned or the unconditioned. Why is this so?
To conceive of conditioned phenomena is to have conceptualization; that which is free from conceptualization is the eye of wisdom.
One who attains this radiance has already transcended all traces of the eye; for this reason, there is nothing seen.
He asked Pu-shou again:
"If the self is accomplished through causes and conditions as being equal [to all things], does the bhikṣu therefore fail to attain the fruit? He replied:
“Brahmā! Could one who lacks equanimity ever attain the realization of the fruit?
Even if they practice according to the equal treatment of all, they will not attain the fruit of realization; it is only by being free from conceptualization that one perceives and attains it.”
"To establish a place for pride is not an impartial remedy; whether one possesses pride or is free from pride, it is not appropriate to set a time limit.
He asked again: "Pūrṇamukha!"
"By what dharma is 'the time of convention' defined, such that one speaks of 'the time of convention'? He replied:
"That dharma which is not born, is not being born now, and will not be born—this is the 'time of convention' of all dharmas; when I speak of the 'time of convention,' I mean this."
He asked Pu-shou again:
"When, in terms of time, does such a birth occur? He replied:
"In this way, with respect to time, that which is non-arising is called 'arising'; to transcend all perceptions of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) is what is termed 'equanimity' (samatā)."
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'equality'? He replied:
"The equality of the self and of nirvāṇa such that they are not two—this is what is called 'equality.
That which is equal has no basis upon which to rely; this is called equality.
That which is expressed as impartiality is called equality."
The absence of gain and loss, of the righteous and the unrighteous—this is called equanimity.
The elimination of all that can be thought upon—this is called equanimity.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Speak these words quickly; it is truly as you have said.

When these words were spoken, seven thousand bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind; twenty-two thousand devaputras became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; ten thousand bhikṣus were freed from craving and desire; two hundred devas and humans resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; and five hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.
Thereupon, the Brahmā deity Dharmacittin addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"Does the youth Mañjuśrī perform the work of a Buddha?
Mañjuśrī immediately replied to the Brahmā:
"If the Buddha does not appear in the world, what would constitute the Dharma?
If no Dharma is established, could there be any abiding?
He then asked Puśya again:
“Does the World-Honored One not transform immeasurable people to bring them to nirvana?
Does the Benevolent One not create benefit and profit for the classes of sentient beings who are beyond calculation?”
He replied: "Brahmā!
Is there not anyone among human beings who would wish to bring about existence?"
He replied, "No. He answered:
"Brahmā! Do you, on the contrary, wish for human beings to achieve the status of a person? He replied:
"No," he replied, "Brahmā!"
"Furthermore, do you wish to cause the Tathāgata— who is unimpeded and non-existent— to arise? He replied, "No!"
He replied: "What kind of human beings are they?
Those whom the Tathāgata has rescued and enabled to attain parinirvāṇa?"
He replied: "Viśeṣacintin!
That Dharma is unarisen;
if one considers it according to what was just said, there is neither birth-and-death nor extinction, and there is nothing to be attained."
He replied: "It is so, Brahmā! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, neither attains birth and death nor enters parinirvāṇa."
Furthermore, Brahmā!
Regarding those śrāvakas liberated through the World-Honored One’s transformation, even in reckoning them, there is neither birth-and-death nor extinction; this itself constitutes their extinction.
Brahmā! What is called "nirvāṇa" is merely a conventional worldly expression, a name established by provisional designation.
What is called "birth and death" is likewise a conventional worldly expression for that which revolves without beginning or end; it, too, has no nirvāṇa.
He replied: "Samantabhadra! Who would ever be willing to believe such words?"
He replied, "It is one who is without attachment to any phenomena.
He then asked Pṛthuśiras again:
"If there is something upon which one relies, what is it that constitutes attachment? He replied, "Brahmā!..."
Whatever one relies upon constitutes attachment to the false and illusory.

Suppose, Brahmā, that one were truly established in the ultimate truth; such a person would have no pride regarding this, nor would they have anything to delight in—how much less would they rely upon or become attached to emptiness?

Therefore, one who perceives the ultimate truth has no attachments; having no attachments, there is no birth-and-death; not being born and dying, yet not departing from birth-and-death—this is what is called "extinction" (nirvāṇa).
He asked Pu-shou again:
"As for those who have attained parinirvāṇa, what was their aspiration in seeking parinirvāṇa? He replied:

“Brahmā! That which is called ‘nirvāṇa’ is named the turning of mutual causes. It is the practice of wisdom through the activities of the various consciousnesses; when all formations (*saṃskāra*) are tranquil and have no point of origin, they have no place of abiding. This absence of a place of abiding is precisely what is called nirvāṇa.
One who acts without a place of abiding is said to be eternally extinguished; this is the time of the summary of the Way. That there is no arising is precisely what is called the Four Noble Truths.”
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Samantagamin asked Puṣya:
"What has been said now is entirely truthful speech. He replied:
“O son of good family!
All that is spoken is entirely truthful.
He then asked Puśya:
"What he speaks of is empty, illusory, and like an echo;
is it nevertheless true? He replied, "It is indeed true."
Why is this so? That which is spoken has no location and nothing upon which it is established; having attained mastery, it is called "truth" (satya), and thus all such speech is entirely truth.

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, likewise speaks the teachings for all those devas and humans; yet, when one calculates these words, they are neither manifold nor different. Why is this so?

All that is spoken is the word of the Tathāgata; all Tathāgatas neither act nor advance or retreat. Whatever words they utter or whatever teachings they expound, all such verbal instructions constitute their teaching.

For this reason, all that is spoken consists of equal characters; by means of these equal characters, one can become one and the same as those characters. Having been able to equalize all characters, one attains mastery and is thus able to be impartial, such that all speech universally practices equality.
He asked Pu-shou again:
"Does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, not distinguish between the speech of the noble ones and the speech of those who are not noble? He replied:
“Virtuous one, do you wish for the assembly of noble sages to be taught by means of words and letters?
Or do you wish for the teaching of the noble sages to be without words and letters? He replied:
"So it is," Pūrṇamukha replied. "Regarding those words of the noble ones,
since there are no such words of the noble ones, can there be any conceptualization?"
He replied, "No! He answered:

"Therefore, written characters possess no conceptualization; if one were to abandon all conceptualization, this is called the noble and holy state being free from verbal expression. Those who are noble and holy do not speak by means of written characters."

There is neither the perception of a person nor the perception of phenomena; it is like musical instruments and the rhythmic beating of a great drum, which produce sound through causes and conditions yet possess no conceptual thought. So too it is with the noble ones: though they manifest what is spoken and employ words, they remain unattached.
He asked Pu-shou again:
"The Tathāgata has said:
'When a gathering is convened, two things should be undertaken: either the discussion of the Dharma, or remaining silent and tranquil like the noble sages.'"
"Regarding that, Samantabhadra, what is meant by 'discussing the Dharma,' and what is meant by 'noble tranquility'? He replied:
"If one does not contend with the Buddha, does not contradict the sūtras and the Dharma, and does not disturb the Sangha, this is what is called 'preaching the Dharma.

If one contemplates the Dharma and sets their mind upon the Buddha, they remain detached from form and desire; for that which is called the Dharma is unconditioned and formless, and that which is called the Sangha consists of the noble and holy ones who are profoundly tranquil."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
To diligently cultivate and practice the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni), and to analyze and understand them—this is the teaching of the Dharma.
To have no mental constructions regarding any phenomena—this is called the tranquil state of the noble ones (ārya)."
“O son of noble family!
Whoever diligently analyzes and explains the four right efforts (catvāri samyakprahāṇāni), this is called discourse on the Dharma.
When one discourses on the Dharma regarding equanimity, neither treating it as equal nor creating any grasping toward it, this is termed the noble tranquility.”
If there is one who reverently practices and expounds upon the four bases of psychic power, this constitutes the discourse on the Dharma;
yet if there is neither body, nor speech, nor mind, it is called the noble stillness.
To reverently practice and explain the five faculties and the five powers constitutes the discourse on the Dharma; yet [if there is no such activity], it is the state beyond words.

Furthermore, if one does not have faith in the Dharma because there is no sound, then there would be no noble ones (ārya) who select and take up the various dharmas, who establish themselves with single-minded diligence, and who equally achieve fundamental liberation. It is by having complete faith in all dharmas, fully understanding and resolving all that is taught, and practicing with wisdom that this is called the liberation of the noble ones.
To follow the sages and be liberated through the seven factors of enlightenment is called the discourse on the Dharma;
to observe form and desire with equanimity, neither elevating nor depressing them—attaining such practice is termed "sage-like tranquility."
To practice with diligent application and understand the Eightfold Noble Path is what is called the "Dharma of Discourse.
Having seen the place of origin of one's spiritual lineage, one is like a floating raft, neither clinging to the Dharma nor clinging to non-Dharma; this is called "Noble Tranquility."
“Noble son, know this: he who understands and realizes the ultimate destination of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is said to be one who discourses on the Dharma.

If one realizes the Dharma through the body, then one does not depart from the body; if one beholds the Dharma, then one does not depart from the Dharma. For one who sees, there is no fundamental seeing; if one does not see duality, then one does not perceive duality. As for that which is seen according to its true nature—that which is seen by present wisdom—is itself non-seeing. This non-seeing is what is called the noble tranquility.”
"Furthermore, son of good family!
To analytically explain that which is not identical with a self, not identical with another, and not identical with dharmas—this is the discourse on the Dharma.

If one does not apprehend a dharma, remains free from all teachings of written words, sounds, and verbal expressions, abandons pride, gives rise to tranquility, and with a mind that is serene, reaches the ultimate in practice—this is called the 'serene state of the noble ones. "
"Furthermore, son of good family!
If other sentient beings and various others each perceive these faculties of people, [the Buddhas] explain them for them through differentiation;
whether their minds are concentrated or distracted, these noble ones remain tranquil, established in composure without any agitation."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Samantacārin asked Pūrṇamukha:

“Regarding what you have just discussed, noble sir, I observe that its ultimate meaning pertains to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; there is no teaching of dharmas, nor is there any noble sage’s tranquility.”
Why is this? Because they are unable to clearly comprehend the fundamental root of sentient beings and fail to investigate equality. Furthermore, Puṣya!
Who could say that he possesses an impartial mind?
Who abides in accordance with the Dharma and dwells in the tranquility of the noble ones?

One should say that it is the Tathāgata who is impartial; for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are able to clearly understand the fundamental nature of sentient beings and remain perpetually concentrated in samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Viśeṣacintin, saying:
"It is indeed as the noble son Samantagamin has said; only the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are able to fully comprehend it."
Thereupon, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"I have personally received this instruction from the Blessed One’s own lips as he told the bhikṣus: 'When you gather and sit together, two things should be undertaken:
first, the discussion of the sūtras;'"
Second, regarding the tranquility of the noble ones (*ārya-śānti*):
if there are members of the *śrāvaka* assembly who do not practice it, for what reason does the Tathāgata speak these words of Dharma for the sake of the *śrāvakas*, saying:
"One should analyze and discourse upon the sūtras; if one does not do so, there is the tranquility of the noble ones"?
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Can the assembly of śrāvakas engage in discourse or practice the tranquil stillness of the noble ones without having anything to ask?"
He replied: "No, indeed! O God among Gods!"
"Therefore, Subhūti, you should form this view:
among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, there is no dharma to be taught; the noble ones are tranquil."
Thereupon, Viśeṣacintin addressed the venerable Subhūti:
"Venerable elder,
do you know the fundamental nature of sentient beings as perceived by the Tathāgata?"
Regarding these eighty-four thousand modes of conduct that have been formulated and explained, would you rather recite them?
Venerable sir, with what wisdom do you contemplate and understand liberation therein?
He replied, “I am not equal to him. The other said:

“You possess a samādhi of fixed intent called ‘Contemplating the Minds of Sentient Beings. One who abides in this samādhi is able to observe and perceive the minds of sentient beings, one’s own mind, and the minds of others, without any obstruction.”
He replied, “I am not equal to him.
Viśeṣacintin spoke again:

“O Subhūti! The Tathāgata speaks of eighty-four thousand practices; these are explained through their various manifestations. Having attained mastery over the samādhi of medical treatment, he remains unshakable and universally knows the minds of all sentient beings. Therefore, Subhūti!”
When you form this contemplation, know that this is not within the reach of the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. "O Subhūti!
There are those who practice lustful conduct who attain liberation by means of the principle of emptiness; the Tathāgata knows them all. If it were not through emptiness;"

Furthermore, there may be someone who acts with anger and perceives faults; the Tathāgata fully knows that such a person attains liberation through their aversion rather than through a mind of loving-kindness.
Or there may be someone who acts with delusion; the Tathāgata fully knows that such a person attains liberation through discourse rather than through the preaching of the Dharma.

Or there may be someone whose conduct is characterized by equal parts [of the three poisons], who does not practice based on emptiness, nor attain liberation through contemplation; who does not transcend the world through loving-kindness, nor through hatred; and who does not attain liberation through exhortation or praise, nor through the preaching of the Dharma.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata fully knows that according to the teachings he imparts in accordance with their conduct and faculties, beings attain liberation through the conditions of their respective types.
Therefore, Subhūti..."
"One should form this contemplation: the Tathāgata’s meditative concentration and exposition of the sublime Dharma are called the 'tranquility of the noble ones' (ārya-śānti).
At that time, Subhūti said to Mañjuśrī:

"Pratyekabuddhas are not capable of expounding the Dharma in this way, nor do they possess the tranquility of the noble ones; only the Bodhisattvas are fully endowed with these qualities, and thus they alone are able to expound the Dharma and [attain] the tranquility of the noble ones."
He replied, “The Tathāgata’s clarity regarding all that he knows is such that there is nothing he does not penetrate.
The World-Honored One said to Subhūti:

“There is a samādhi called ‘Entering All Sounds to Rectify the Distracted Mind. By means of this samādhi, the bodhisattva enters into correct meditative absorption and practice, universally perfecting all virtues and fully preparing all modes of conduct.”
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Samantamukha asked the Bodhisattva Samantacara: "Noble son!
To expound the eighty-four thousand modes of conduct and the eighty-four thousand various treasuries of teachings is what is called preaching the Dharma."
To thoroughly understand all perceptions up to the state of cessation and tranquility—this is called the "tranquility of the noble ones" (*ārya-śānti*).
Furthermore, son of good family!
If a Buddha were to spend one eon, or even more than an eon, analyzing and resolving the meaning of this taught Dharma—this is called the "tranquility of the noble ones."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Samantagamin, saying: "Noble son!

In the distant past, beyond incalculable kalpas—immeasurable, limitless, and inconceivable—there was a Buddha named Samantaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, who appeared in the world during the kalpa called Yaśas and in the world-system called Priyadarśana."

In the world of Lovely-to-See belonging to the Tathāgata Samantaprabha, the harvests are abundant, the land is peaceful and secure, and grain is cheap and plentiful. Free from affliction and full of joy, gods and humans flourish there.

That Buddha-world has a ground composed of all kinds of jewels, perfumed by various fragrant trees; it is soft, fine, and exquisite like a wondrous robe, and is further adorned with lotus flowers made of various precious gems.

"In the world-system of Priyadarśana, there are four hundred billion four-continent worlds (*cāturdvīpaka*). Each of these four continents measures three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li* in extent. Each city wall is forty thousand *li* in length and breadth, and all are naturally adorned with precious jewels."

Each of these great cities comprised twenty districts (*jana-pada*) as its administrative units, along with various counties and towns; each great city was governed by a sovereign who presided over countless hundreds of thousands of inhabitants.

Furthermore, whatever those people behold with their own eyes, they see only that which is beautiful, pleasing, agreeable, and worthy of reverence; all the people therein attain the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha. For this reason, that Buddha-world is named "Beloved Vision."
If various bodhisattvas travel to other buddha-lands, they do not take pleasure in those other worlds.

If the Tathāgata Samantaprabhā teaches the doctrine of the three vehicles, preaching the sūtras and dharmas for the sake of the śrāvakas, and extensively and with great care explains their meanings, then he will give rise to two practices to proclaim and expound the dharma: the practice of the noble tranquility.

“In the eastern world, there are two bodhisattvas residing in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja. One is named Kāmaśeṣa and the other is named Dhāraṇīmati. They went to the presence of the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa, prostrated themselves upon the ground, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood with palms joined.”
That Buddha-world is named Pure Universal Exposition of Samādhi; it is called "Pure" for a single reason.
If a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they abandon all conceptualizations and defilements, and immediately obtain the radiance of the Buddha-dharma; for this reason, the world is named Pure.
All phenomena of the past are entirely pure; all phenomena of the future are also entirely pure; and all phenomena of the present are likewise entirely pure—this is called the two kinds of purity.
"The reason it is called 'pure' is that it refers to true purity. True purity neither arises nor is there anything to be purified.
That which is pure is pure from its very source; therefore, it is called 'fundamentally pure. This fundamental purity is all phenomena."
What dharma is fundamentally pure?
Emptiness is fundamentally pure, for it is utterly detached from all things.
All dharmas are entirely illusory; non-conceptualization is fundamentally pure.
Furthermore, all dharmas consist in the elimination of all conceptualizations; the matters of wrong thought are entirely extinguished, and that which is wishless is fundamentally pure.

All dharmas are not to be practiced; they are without aspiration and capable of ultimate fulfillment. Because they are free from inherent nature and are fundamentally pure, this is called "fundamental purity manifest" and "fundamental purity radiant."
"Just as birth-and-death is pure, so too is Nirvana fundamentally pure;
just as Nirvana is pure, so too are all dharmas fundamentally pure.
This is what is called 'fundamental purity.'"
The luminosity of the mind is like this, son of good family!

Just as space has no location and no object of aspiration, if one can thoroughly treat the afflictions, the fundamental purity of the mind—having neither location nor object of seeking—is able to eliminate the desires of the afflictions.

"This son of good family, the mind is fundamentally pure and its nature is luminous. It is like space, which is not harmed by clouds, mist, smoke, or dust; it is neither destroyed nor illuminated by them. Space is fundamentally pure, incapable of being defiled, and free from affliction; because it is ultimately untainted, it is called 'space.'"

If one contemplates in accordance with reality, the foolish and ignorant commoner speaks of afflictions (*kleśa*); yet the fundamental purity of the mind has no place that can be defiled, for it cannot be defiled. Therefore, it is called "pure from beginning to end. Because it is not stained, it is called "fundamentally pure," and thus liberation is truly liberation.
“O son of good family!
One enters universally and equally into the pure world.
At that time, for the sake of the bodhisattvas, the World-Honored One expounded this samādhi in detail; upon hearing it, their minds then incline toward the radiance of the light of the Dharma.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Exhausting the Intent addressed the Tathāgata Universal Radiance:
“I have previously heard, O God among Gods!
Regarding this universal entry, by what skillful means should one practice it?”
The Buddha Samantaprabhāsa told the Bodhisattva Kṣayamati:
"O noble ones who have come here, sons of good family!
You should practice two courses of conduct."
"What are these two? They are the analytical teaching of the Dharma and the practice of the noble ones, which is tranquil and serene.
"Furthermore, son of good family!"

Having heard this from the World-Honored One, that bodhisattva prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and immediately withdrew. He soon arrived at a separate pleasure grove and proceeded to practice there within a constructed pavilion.

At that time, there was a Brahmā named Suprabha, who, together with seventy-two thousand devas and Brahmās, went to the Bodhisattva and prostrated at his feet. Having seen him, he immediately asked the Bodhisattva:

"Noble son, has the Tathāgata Samantaprabha gathered this assembly? As the bhikṣus sit here, you also preach the sūtra, saying that two things should be practiced: the analytical exposition of the Dharma, and the noble and holy tranquility free from discursive thought."
"O son of noble family!
What is meant by 'preaching the Dharma' and 'the sage’s tranquility'?
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to the Brahma-king Suprabha:
“Brahmā, listen! I shall answer your question briefly.
The Tathāgata perceives through direct vision and explains with discernment, crossing over to the ultimate limit.”
"Yes, noble son! For that assembly of bodhisattvas, you should extensively explain the meaning of these two phrases.

At that time, seventy-two thousand Brahmā devas all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and the bodhisattva Suprabha attained the Samādhi of Universal Radiance.
"Yes, son of good family! These bodhisattvas cannot be restrained;

they give rise to unimpeded eloquence and pose difficult questions. Who is it that preaches the Dharma? The noble ones remain in tranquility yet expound it forth. For seventy-six thousand years they have proclaimed two phrases and sent them forth, yet they could not find the limit or boundary of even a single phrase, let alone two."
At that time, the Tathāgata, dwelling in mid-air, spoke these words: "Stop,
son of good family!"
Do not engage in speech that gives rise to contention or dispute.

Upon hearing these parables and all that is spoken, one should be liberated by means of them—just as an echo arises from a call—and thus follow accordingly, entering through the echo. As for those with eloquence who possess discernment, their inexhaustible conduct cannot be fully exhausted.

In the brief moment since I first resolved my mind, were it for an eon or even more than an eon, if one were to praise the noble eloquence of that questioner regarding its meaning, one could never reach the end nor find its limit.
“O worthy ones, you cannot exhaust the wisdom of eloquence; furthermore, it is again and again tranquility.
The Buddha said:
“To be silent and serene, without the affairs of words or conventional propriety, and not to seek gain or offerings as a benefit—this is what constitutes propriety.”
Furthermore, one should mindfully recognize the intent of those whom one rescues.
When one hears an explanation from the Tathāgata, one should then remain silent.
Therefore, son of good family!
In a single thought-moment, a bodhisattva can extol and expound upon the eloquence manifested over hundreds of thousands of kalpas; only after practicing this should one form such a thought.

There was a bodhisattva named Weiwei Jiuhu Jinyi (Majestic Protector of the Exhausted Mind) who, dwelling among humans, spoke these words concerning the ground entered by the Universal Practice Brahmā and the two bodhisattvas.
When reflecting upon the past, could it be that they were anyone other than yourself?
Do not entertain such a view. Why is this so?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kṣepaṇabuddhi was none other than the present Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra;
the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara was the present Samantagupta;
and the Brahmā Śubhaprabha was the present Brahmā Cittadhara.
Chapter Nine: Diligent Practice (3). Chapter Nine, "Diligent Practice. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Samantagamin addressed the Buddha, the Great Sage, saying:
"It is most unprecedented, O God among Gods!"

The Tathāgatas, the World-Honored Ones, possess such sublime virtue and majesty that they are able to attain such great benefit and meaning; this is due to their constant diligence and exertion through vigor. As for those who are indolent, what can even hundreds of thousands of Buddhas do for them?
"So be it, World-Honored One!
Those who seek the Way should be single-mindedly diligent.
Then the youth Prabhūtaratna asked Samantagāmin:
“O noble son! Are you able to distinguish and know what practice is called the diligent exertion of a bodhisattva? He replied:
"If a bodhisattva who practices according to the rules observes the proper timing, they should have no discursive thoughts and not abandon their diligent effort.
He asked again:
"What is meant by diligent effort that observes the proper timing and yet remains free from discursive thought?"
He replied: "If a practitioner does not conceptualize any phenomena, then at that time, the seasons are without thought.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'acting according to the occasion without mental preoccupation'? He replied:
"If one is able to practice all dharmas fully and perceives their equality, that constitutes acting according to the occasion, and there is no mental preoccupation."
He asked again:
"Is it possible to cause seeing and the other [faculties] to function? He replied:
"No. If one perceives equality, one immediately falls into the sixty-two views; that is not true equality.
The Brahma-Devaputra Dharmanirnaya asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
“Regarding that which is equal: is it called ‘equality’ because one does not perceive any phenomena?
Viśeṣacintin replied, “For what reason, Brahmā, do you not perceive them?”
He replied: "One does not have views because of the removal of two things; that which has no object of vision is what constitutes equal vision.
He asked again:
"Is it by being in the Brahma palace that one attains right view? He replied,
"What constitutes 'view'?"

He replied: "That which is perceived is like form (rūpa), having no fundamental basis and not being produced through differentiation; yet it is as if there were something perceived. Likewise, sensation (vedanā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) have no fundamental basis and are likewise without differentiation."
“Furthermore, Subhūti, if one perceives the five aggregates as being without a fundamental basis, this constitutes a manifestation within the world; it is the vision of equality.
He asked again:
“What is it that you practice while residing in the Brahma palace?”
He replied: "To exhaust all marks (lakṣaṇa) is this practice; this, Mañjuśrī, is the practice of worldly convention.
He asked again:
"If all marks are extinguished, yet there remains the mark of the worldly mind, how can one exhaust the practice of mental marks?
He replied: "Puruṣottama!..."
"The characteristics of the world are not to be exhausted.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'discriminating as the practice of various characteristics' and 'the practice of the world'?"
He replied: "That which is completely exhausted has nothing further to be exhausted; that which still has something left to exhaust cannot be fully exhausted.
He asked again:
“Brahmā! Did not the Tathāgata, the Arhat, not say that the exhaustion of phenomena refers to conditioned things? He replied:
"That which is the dharma of exhaustion has never been exhausted again; the Tathāgata has said:
'That which is the dharma of exhaustion refers to conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma). He asked again:
“Brahmā! What is meant by ‘conditioned phenomena’? He replied:
"That which exhausts phenomena is called the conditioned.
He asked again: "Brahmā!..."
"What is the basis upon which conditioned phenomena are established? He replied:
"When one abides in the state of the unconditioned and spontaneity, that is the basis for the conditioned."
He asked again:
"Regarding these dharmas, both conditioned and unconditioned, what is their distinction? He replied:

Regarding all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, there are distinctions spoken of according to worldly conventions; thus, worldly discourse designates some as "conditioned" and others as "unconditioned. Yet, between these conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena, there is no difference, for phenomena possess no distinction whatsoever.
He asked again:
"Brahmā! What is meant by that which is called 'Dharma'?"
He replied: "That which is called 'Dharma' is without differentiation; this is what is meant by Dharma.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'speech'? He replied:
"That which involves entrusting something or that which involves expounding something—this is called speech."

Why is this so? All verbal expressions possess the same characteristic; the Tathāgata discerns them as equal. That which is spoken does not constitute differentiation; therefore, it is called "verbal expression."
Furthermore, Pu-shou!
All that is spoken is non-speaking; this is called "that which cannot be attained. That which the Buddha speaks as "equal enlightenment" involves no acquisition and no verbal expression.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'the thoughts and practices of a Samyaksaṃbuddha'? He replied:
"One does not engage with form, does not engage with signs, and does not engage with phenomena.
He asked again:
"When one preaches the Dharma regarding signs that are difficult to attain, is this a practice of mental recollection?"
He replied: "No!

That which possesses marks is a dharma that has no fundamental basis; it lacks reality and is not without differentiation. This is what the Tathāgata contemplates and practices. His practice is non-practice; it has no fundamental basis, nothing to be explained, and nothing to be lost."
He asked again:
"Brahmā! How does the Tathāgata achieve equal enlightenment?"
He replied: "Viśeṣacintin!

The Tathāgata understands that all phenomena are fundamentally pure and naturally without origin; having attained equal enlightenment, he is therefore designated as the 'Equally Enlightened One' (Samyaksaṃbuddha)."
Chapter Ten: Aspiration for the Mahāyāna (3). Chapter Ten: Aspiration for the Mahāyāna. At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantacārin addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What is meant, Great Sage, by the name 'Bodhisattva aspiring to the Mahāyāna'? How should one contemplate this?"
The World-Honored One replied to Samantagupta in verse:
"If one aspires to seek the Buddha-way, One has never craved for form;
As it is with form, so it is with the Way— This is what it means to aspire to the Way with the mind."
Form is no different from the Path; the practitioner is likewise so.
When one's aspirations are unimpaired, that is the supreme wisdom of the Path.
The meaning of the Path is the meaning of non-destruction; the Path has no meaning of gain.
To cultivate the ultimate truth is to be one who aspires to seek the Way.
To seek the Buddha-way within the aggregates (skandhas), the elements (dhātus), and the sense bases (āyatanas)—to understand these is to be an Equal Awakened One;
there is no distinction between such a person and the Way itself.
If one does not grasp at phenomena, there is no superior, inferior, or intermediate;
nor is there anything to be discarded—this is the aspiration for the Way.
Whether it be dharma or non-dharma, do not conceive of these two things.
Because one does not grasp at these two conditions, one is said to be seeking the Way with resolve;
where there is conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta*), there are two things, but where there is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there are no two.
Abandoning the affairs of discrimination is what constitutes the practice of the Way.
Yet he delivers ordinary beings, abiding in profound stillness;
without attaining the fruits of the noble ones, he is the World’s Benefactor, free from attachment.
Observing the phenomena of the world, he dwells amidst the mundane like a lotus flower.
To practice the noble and sublime conduct is to be intent on seeking the Way;
wherever one wanders in the world, one performs deeds therein.
While worldly people are bound by attachments, the wise and enlightened are liberated.
Fearless in the cycle of birth and death, the bodhisattva’s resolve and nature are strong;
without cowardice and steadfast, they practice the Buddha-way.
Should they be one who understands clearly, they discern the nature of phenomena.
Regarding both the Dharma and non-Dharma, they have no conceptualizations whatsoever.
Without abandoning or departing from all phenomena, they practice the Buddha-way with single-minded devotion;
they never fall away, for that Way is free from conceptualization.
All dharmas are without marks, comparable to empty space;
Neither marked nor unmarked—those who possess clarity do not dwell upon this.
In practice, they employ courageous skillful means; This is the perfection of skillful expedient (upāya-pāramitā).
Thus causing other sentient beings to fulfill their aspirations and joys;
always upholding the True Dharma and abiding in equanimity— this is the True Dharma,
wherein one remains within the scriptures free from manifold thoughts.
Although the Buddhas appear in the world, they do not arise from anywhere;
they abide eternally in the True Dharma—this is how one can honor the scriptures.
All phenomena manifest before us, whether they accord with the Dharma or are contrary to it.
What has been taught is likewise thus: one then abides in the rootless.
Following and practicing the subtle and wondrous path, yet not perceiving the deeds of Māra—even regarding all phenomena in this way, one does not receive the teachings of the Path.
If one aspires to the Buddha-way yet establishes pride in their practice, there will be no teaching of wisdom, and what is spoken will yield no attainment.
The wisdom of all Buddhas is immeasurable; regarding phenomena, they do not cling to phenomena.
Having no reliance upon those things, one crosses to the other shore by this path.
With the will set on the Way through giving, and with a mind that delights in renunciation,
one subdues all states of existence and remains unattached even to the Buddha-way.
The Dharma cannot be excelled, nor can it be received as a gift;
all phenomena are likewise so. One does not grasp at the mental image [of them], thereby attaining ultimate liberation and comprehending all dharmas.
Those who cultivate the verse of compassion are free from all views;
for those who conceive of a self, there is no duality.
They do not dwell in arrogance, nor do they long for anything that exists.
Practicing all forms of giving, they encourage and assist in the Buddha-way.
Regarding both giving and the path of virtue, they do not dwell on the duality of existence;
observing the precepts without [clinging to] their practice, they always stand firm in the Right Path.
Furthermore, they harbor no conceptual thoughts, saying, "I have established the precepts.
Being unconditioned and unarisen, the noble ones thoroughly understand the precepts;
therefore, their precepts are pure, and their unraveling of fetters is like space.
The body is like a reflection in a mirror; speech is like the echo of a call.
To understand the mind as being like an illusion and not to harbor pride regarding precepts and mindfulness—this is to follow the Teacher’s instruction; such a person delights in profound stillness.
Eliminating all evils is the perfection of serenity.
That which is called the prohibitive precepts has no duality;
by fully discerning the nature of phenomena, these precepts are untainted.
The perfection of patience endures all afflictions;
likewise for all sentient beings, one establishes them in equanimity.
Without relying on empty space, one realizes that all phenomena have no place of abiding.
He has no reviling, nor does he have anything at all;
even if his body were to be dismembered limb by limb, his mind harbors no anger or resentment.
His mind dwells nowhere, nor does it abide within or without.
Observing oneself as one establishes the fourfold assembly, if one can endure enemies and foes,
never committing evil deeds, and practicing patience like the earth,
bringing this very state into the present— this is what is called "patience."
All these sentient beings cannot cause them to give rise to anger;
they encourage and assist others in delighting in the Mahāyāna.
Possessing great power and being fearless, whatever their minds and intentions engage with, they have never been attached to anything.
Since the very beginning of the primordial limit, birth and death have been unknowable;
therefore, for the sake of a single person, I vow to don the armor of great power.
Since this Dharma has never arisen, how could it ever be subject to destruction?
The power of the place of inversion does not comprehend the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
Various kinds of divine eyes are established; the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inconceivable.
One who understands it thus does not give rise [to views] and has nothing that can be exhausted.
Sentient beings do not understand this— The nature of all phenomena and what is non-dharmic.
They constantly exert themselves in these meanings, Yet, through delusion and negligence, The Buddhas cannot enter them; Ultimately, they possess nothing at all.
Constantly donning the armor of non-action, he observes the distinctions of diligence;
selecting all phenomena as being like illusions or mirages,
he perceives them as lacking any solid essence, just as one gazes upon empty space.
To contemplate what is false is to cling to that which is of no benefit.
Therefore, it is said that through equanimity one attains nirvana;
by means of this meaning of diligence, practice it so that it remains unimpaired.
In the practice of what is to be practiced, one is free from further practice; diligence is supreme.
The practice of the Path is tranquility, and one should cultivate the meaning of emptiness.
Do not trust in the false and deceptive; let your mind stand in awe of birth and death.
Valiant and delighting in secluded dwelling, clearly perceiving impermanence as like a desolate wilderness,
the wise find joy in dhyāna; through the *abhijñā* of the Infinite,
they remain as if gathered in solitude, their resolve abiding in equanimity.
With dignified deportment free from conceptual thought, his mind is always in constant concentration;
fundamentally pure and equal to the Dharma, he is tranquil and free from all outflows.
Having faith and delight in liberation, he remains eternally in equanimous concentration regarding deliverance.
This impartiality is embraced and maintained, always abiding in equanimity.
Without the conflict or disorder of partiality, it is therefore called "evenness.
Not being deluded by mental views, the mind of the Way is universally pervasive.
To transform and enlighten all sentient beings— therefore it is called equality;
To constantly mind the Buddhas— the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body,
unattached to form— therefore it is called equality.
When practicing the conduct of the sūtras, whether regarding what is Dharma or non-Dharma, the mind has no object of thought; therefore, it is called equanimity.
When the mind contemplates the Noble Assembly, one realizes that the assembly is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Detached from both the calculable and the incalculable, they are clearly proficient in meditative concentration;
they universally behold all Buddha-lands and all sentient beings of the ten directions.
Within their eyes there is no form, and they do not conceive of the duality of existence and non-existence.
Whether hearing all the Buddhas preaching the sutras and dharmas,
they do not, by means of auditory sounds, regress into dualistic conceptions.
They know the minds of all sentient beings with a single mind.
Without self and without intention, there are no manifold perceptions.
Though one’s consciousness and mindfulness extend across hundreds of millions of koṭis of kalpas—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—there is neither before nor after; such is that which is known.
Traveling through billions of lands, he manifests infinite miraculous powers;
at that time, this wise one’s body, speech, and mind remain undisturbed.
Able to discern the scriptures, his eloquence is peerless.
Though he expounds for billions of kalpas, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is never lost.
With the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), he skillfully understands the five aggregates;
practicing without conceptual play, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of others.
Thoroughly understanding the conditions of causes and effects, one abandons all that is conceptually discriminated;
because of the afflictions of the world, one then realizes all that is pure.
Through these causes and conditions, one attains liberation, and thus there are no longer any views.
Thus understanding all matters, one sees that all phenomena are without form or image.
One beholds the Buddha-body for oneself and, contemplating emptiness, is able to endure it all;
seeing the cessation of both beginning and end, one realizes that nothing whatsoever exists.
Realizing that the essence of wisdom is fundamentally pure, one has no thoughts regarding the world;
by departing from the masses of darkness and obscurity, one then practices the way of the Path.
This vehicle is the Great Vehicle; the Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable.
He cares for and illuminates all sentient beings, exhorting them toward this Unsurpassed Vehicle;
when one calculates all paths, this vehicle is the most honored.
Thus, regarding that vehicle, they fully understand all its trainings.
Even if all people were unable to limit this vehicle,
we who belong to the Mahāyāna listen and reflect in order to deliver all living beings.
Those who establish their resolve in the Mahāyāna are like space itself.
Never having had lustful desire, they are without attachment toward sentient beings.
Just as space is boundless and without limit, formless and invisible, so too is the Mahāyāna: limitless and free from outflows.
Even if all people were to set their minds upon this vehicle and undergo its training in such a manner, this vehicle would remain preeminent.
Even if one were to practice according to this vehicle for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, [it remains unsurpassed].
One cannot exhaustively praise its virtues; the merit and blessings of the Mahāyāna abandon all obstacles, and through wisdom one attains mastery.
If someone should uphold this sublime sūtra and recite these verses,
They shall never fall into the evil realms, but thereafter attain liberation.
Whether in the heavens or among humans, those who revere this sutra likewise shall receive my prediction of their enlightenment, so that they may all attain the Way of the Buddha.
Those who hear this sutra will have no fear at the end;
possessing this true Dharma, they shall be established in the sublime doctrine.
They will then turn the wheel of the Dharma, abiding in this sutra in such a manner.
One who reflects upon all things and turns back from birth and death is close to equal and right awakening; such is the way one upholds this sutra.
One who grasps and maintains this sutra possesses immense and heroic power.
Having subdued the armies of Māra, he advances greatly with boundless wisdom;
just like the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he receives the prediction and attains the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti).
To those who revere this sutra, I too shall grant a prediction.
"The Buddhas have no other means of arising than this; the World-Saviors, Protectors, Roarers, and Guides—if one expounds this sutra, one thereby performs the work of a Buddha.

When the Buddha spoke these verses, ten thousand devaputras resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi); two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (anutpāda-dharma-kṣānti); the minds of a thousand bhikṣus were liberated as their outflows were exhausted (āsrava-kṣaya); and thirty-two thousand people became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the Dharma-eye (dharma-cakṣur-utpanna).
Chapter Eleven: On the Practice of the Path (3). Chapter Eleven: On the Practice of the Path. At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Today, as I reflect upon what the Great Sage has taught and analyze its meaning, those who have the aspiration and vow to seek the Buddha-way are, in fact, yearning for false views!"
Why is this so? Indeed, World-Honored One!

It is precisely because of attaining false views that one reaches the Buddha-way; for it is by desiring to obtain something that one generates the aspiration, and thus through skillful means, one arrives at false views.
Why is this so? O God among Gods!

Furthermore, one sees that the Way does not abide in the realm of desire, does not abide in the realm of form, and does not abide in the formless realm; since the Way has no place of abiding, for this reason one should not form aspirations toward it.
It is, for example, like a man who takes a piece of iron and places it in a fire; he does not desire the fire and ought not to touch it with his hand. Why is this?
Because it would burn his hand.
Fire does not burn itself; it is only that which takes [fuel] that is burned. Likewise, those who possess the aspiration and seek the Buddha-way are merely seeking fire and burning themselves.
Thus it is, World-Honored One!
The Way has no aspiration or seeking to cross over these two matters, for it has no destination.
It is like a man who resolves to travel through space, thinking, "I wish to walk upon the air," yet that person is unable to walk in space.
Pūrṇa further said:

"There is nothing that can be established within empty space; likewise, for one who has realized the meaning of the Way as being like empty space, the Way has no place of abiding, and thus they transcend duality."

If a bodhisattva establishes the resolve for enlightenment without dualistic conceptions, yet were there a bodhisattva who gives rise to dualistic conceptions while seeking Buddhahood—whether by recollecting the Buddha-way or recollecting its beginning and end—if they recollect the Way, they are recollecting wrong views; and if they recollect the Way or recollect nirvana, they are not a bodhisattva, nor are they practicing the Way.
Thereupon, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin asked Mañjuśrī:
"By what practice does a bodhisattva accord with the practice of the Way? He replied:

“Brahmā! If there is a bodhisattva who practices all dharmas, yet practices nothing at all regarding any signs, this is what it means for a bodhisattva to revere the practice of the Way and transcend the nature of all practices. This, Brahmā, is what is called—”
"One who is a bodhisattva honors and pursues the practice of the Way.
He then asked Pu-shou:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva transcending all realms of conditioned activity and reverently cultivating the practice of the Way?"

He replied: "By being detached from all attachments and all mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and by likewise setting aside the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—one who practices in this way transcends the realm of formations."
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'transcending and crossing over'? He replied:
"To be equal toward the vehicles is to transcend them; to be equal toward all dharmas is the Way itself.
Dhāraṇīcitta then asked:
"How does the Way abide as a skillful means for the practitioner?"
He replied, "It is like that Way.
He asked again:
"What is that path? He replied, "Brahmā!
Furthermore, that Way has no past, future, or present; therefore, the Bodhisattva purifies the three spheres and abides in the Buddha-way.

Whether as in the past, as in the future, or as in the present, when the mind has no destination, there is no thought of practice. One who abides thus has no place of abiding, yet abides universally in all things. One who abides in this manner attains the penetration of all supernormal wisdoms.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'all-encompassing wisdom'? He replied:
"To fully comprehend all things without forming a conceptualization of them is therefore called 'universal penetrating wisdom' (sarvābhijñājñāna).
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'wisdom' (prajñā)?"
He replied: "It is because wisdom is without differentiation and without divergent thoughts; furthermore, it is because all that belongs to sentient beings is likewise, entirely without distinction."
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'sentient beings'? He replied:
“Their names are fundamentally pure and sentient beings are tranquil; for this reason their names are fundamentally pure, and sentient beings are likewise without distinction.
If one were to conceive of distinctions in the Way or differences among sentient beings, one would not be in accord with the Way.”
If the Path is thus, so too are sentient beings; for this reason, there is no distinction, and thus one cannot establish a distinction between them.
Furthermore, my self and the Path are also equal; because the Path is equal, my self is also equal. For this reason, there is no difference whatsoever.
Why is this? Sentient beings have no self and possess no body; therefore, they are without distinction, just as the body has no difference. All dharmas are likewise so.
Dharmamati asked again:
"The Tathāgata’s words are sincere and without falsehood; it is for this reason that he has analyzed these various dharmas. He replied:
“The Tathāgata never discriminates when teaching the Dharma. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata does not apprehend any dharmas; how much less could he discriminate among them?”
He asked again:
"Does the Tathāgata not teach the Dharma of the present?
Is this then the conditioned, or is it the unconditioned? Is this worldly affairs, or is it the practice that transcends the world?"
He replied: "What is the destination?
Who is it that here discriminates bodily formations or verbal instructions?"
He replied, “No! Viśeṣacintin asked again:
"Is that which is called 'body' produced and then utterly extinguished? He replied, "No!"
He replied, “It is so, Brahmā!
That which is called the teaching of the Dharma is, in fact, the teaching of space; and that which is the absence of teaching is likewise so.”
Regarding those dharmas that can be expressed through verbal teaching, dharmas neither arise nor cease; this absence of verbal expression constitutes the verbal teaching of dharmas.
Even if there were no dharmas and no verbal teaching, that would be silence.
Why is this so? Just as with the teachings on all phenomena, so too is the teaching of non-utterance; therefore, it is called the "teaching of that which cannot be spoken.
That in which the Tathāgata dwells is a dwelling nowhere; because there is no dwelling, it is said to be without origin.

12. Chapter on Praise (3). Chapter Twelve: On Praise. Thereupon, the gods of the Four Great Kings, Śakra, and Brahmā Sahāmpati came to the assembly. They made offerings by scattering celestial flowers over the Buddha, and having completed their salutations, they spoke these words:

"If sons of good family or daughters of good family, upon hearing the Dharma taught by the youth Mañjuśrī, should rejoice with faith, they will thereby subdue Māra and the various heterodox teachers."
Why is this? It is because they have abandoned all conceptualizations of views.

If, upon hearing the exposition of this profound and wondrous Dharma, they are neither terrified, nor afraid, nor filled with dread, they are established by all Buddhas; wherever this Dharma flows, that land is where the Tathāgata dwells.
Those who hear this Dharma should regard that as the turning of the wheel of Dharma.

If they travel and wander through commanderies, kingdoms, villages, hamlets, counties, districts, and great states, and behold where this sutra is being disseminated, they will never provide an opportunity for Māra to gain the upper hand; they shall neither be deluded nor dependent on anything, for they have already fully cultivated their practices throughout past ages.
"If there are people who hear the name of this sutra with their ears, they shall not seek parinirvāṇa through the status of a bhikṣu, nor shall they be affected by the works of Māra;
they shall receive this sutra. Indeed, World-Honored One!"

Regarding this sutra, if we attain the illumination of the Dharma, we shall all believe it and dare not transgress or lose the teachings of the Tathāgata, Mañjuśrī, and Brahmā. Should we behold that Dharma-preacher, we shall regard him as if seeing the World-Honored One; we shall listen to and receive the scriptural canon from him and attend upon the Dharma-preacher.
This son of noble family shall always be protected by the various devas.

Should there be anyone who obtains this sutra, copies it, reads, recites, and upholds it, they will be accompanied by countless thousands of sons of the gods, who will all go together to hear and receive what is taught within the assembly.
Chapter Thirteen: Praising Virtue (3). Chapter Thirteen: Praising Virtue. At that time, the World-Honored One praised the great assembly as well as Śakra and Brahmā, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

Excellent! It is just as you have said: even if one were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and offer them in alms, the merit of anyone who hears this Dharma of the sutra would surpass that blessing.
The Buddha said:

"Setting aside these three thousand great thousandfold worlds filled with precious jewels, even if one were to take seven treasures filling as many worlds as there are sands in the Ganges to cultivate merit, it would not equal the merit of one who hears this sutra-dharma for a second time; the root of that merit far surpasses the former."

Noble sons and noble daughters, should they be able to hear this sutra—even if it be for the sake of gain and sustenance, or for the sake of honor and beauty, or for the sake of wealth and occupation, or for the sake of their retinue—they shall become masters of the Dharma and be reborn in the heavens.

Whether one seeks abundance while among humans; whether for the sake of heterodox arts and strange doctrines; whether seeking renown, extensive learning, or great erudition; or if one’s resolve is set on sovereignty and the aspiration to attain firm wisdom; if one seeks the supernormal powers and the three types of penetrating knowledge (*trividyā*); if one desires to acquire all the merits of wholesome dharmas; if, with a mind of awakening, one establishes sentient beings so that they are free from suffering and affliction; or if one seeks the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—sons and daughters of noble family should hear this sutra, receive and uphold it, recite it, and explain it extensively for others. I have never seen anyone who receives this sutra and practices it with a sincere heart who fails to obtain its fruit.
"Now the Buddha earnestly entrusts this to you all.

If there should be anyone who hears this sutra from others, or receives and upholds it from a teacher or preceptor, the Buddha does not see anyone in all the worlds, nor among worldly offerings, who can honor and revere them in a way that repays their kindness."
Why is this so? The Dharma for transcending the world cannot be fully realized through worldly sustenance.

The Dharma for transcending the world cannot be compared to the offerings of the mundane world; thus, one has no attachment to the world. Worldly dharmas cannot be purified to completion, nor can they be attained through mere toil or hope; they cannot be fully realized through the pursuit of worldly offerings. All karmic retributions involve cycles of repetition, yet this sutra is free from such variations. Retribution follows the cycles as described by the Dharma; to transcend such restless wandering and have nothing further to practice—this is true practice. To achieve this is to show reverence to the Dharma Master, and it is to purify and complete all requitals of gratitude.

"If one enters the commanderies, kingdoms, districts, and towns, and through the practice of wearing [the robes] and the implements of alms-gathering, brings many to the merit of liberation—such as these who uphold the Tathāgata’s teaching and cultivate it according to his commands shall attain transcendence. Surpassing the manifold darkness, they raise the victory banners; such as these are courageous and capable of combat, subduing many; they are like lions, free from all terrors; they are like dragon-elephants, having restrained their own minds; they are like seers and immortals, whose words are most sincere."

"Transcending all heterodox and erroneous teachings, they act as skilled physicians to heal all ailments; they preach the profound and wondrous Dharma without fearing hardships. Through such giving, they relinquish all defilements and thereby uphold the pure precepts; remaining tranquil and serene, they cross over to the ultimate limit. Having detached from the self and all that belongs to the body, they exercise great vigor until they reach the unconditioned."

"Throughout incalculable eons, weary of the cycle of birth and death, they delight in meditative concentration and possess single-mindedness; for the sake of great wisdom, they are able to discern all chapters and phrases."

One who thoroughly understands and manifests the meaning of all wisdom is a person of great virtue; possessing hundreds of thousands of incalculable merits, adorned by their own marks, and with wisdom that is inexhaustible, they then eclipse the light of the sun and moon, becoming one of great power.

Regarding the essential power of the dhāraṇī of the ten powers, those of such a kind constitute a great cloud; they proclaim the thunderous sound of the Dharma and pour down the rain of the Great Dharma, thereby able to extinguish all afflictions.
"Having first attained the foremost unconditioned nirvana, one protects against birth and death and soothes away all fears; one becomes a lamp of light that illuminates the manifold darknesses.

Fearing and loathing the net of Māra, one provides rescue so that others may find refuge; one becomes a means of deliverance for all sentient beings; one dwells at the Bodhi tree and attains the Dharma-eye, thereby perceiving that all phenomena are without origin."

“Having thoroughly understood the dharma of emptiness, one establishes great compassion; by abiding in boundless loving-kindness, one attains intimacy with all sentient beings, causing them to turn away from inferior vehicles and head toward the Great Vehicle.”

He burns away all inversions and destroys that which is not yet equal; transcending names and designations, he raises up the titles of virtue, thereby establishing the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and subduing the various māras.
Having attained mastery within the realms of the māras, he turns the wheel of Dharma and summons the worthy ones.

Even if a Buddha were to spend an eon, or even more than an eon, extolling and praising the deeds of this noble being, he could not reach their ultimate limit; such is the loftiness of his merit and the nature of his sublime joy. Only the Tathāgata, with his perfect eloquence, is able to sing the praises of those who uphold this Dharma.

Chapter 14: On Equal Practice (3). Chapter Fourteen: On Equal Practice. At that time, within that assembly, there was a devaputra named Manifesting Non-retrogression who addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What is meant by one who reveres the Dharma and follows the scriptures?"
The World-Honored One replied, “Son of Heaven!
If you wish to know what it means to honor the Dharma and follow the scriptures, it is to be able to revere and accord with all dharmas; this is precisely what is called honoring and following.”
If one can honor and comply with all dharmas, this is called the devoted cultivation of the Dharma. Why is this so?

One who does not honor or comply with any dharmas neither constructs dharmas nor fails to construct them; whatever they do is as if they have done nothing. This is what is called the devoted cultivation of the Dharma.
If one does not cultivate various roots of wholesome virtue, yet is likewise without unwholesomeness—this is called practicing the Dharma.

It is neither with outflows nor without outflows; it is neither guilty nor guiltless; it is neither mundane nor supramundane; it is neither with form nor without form; it is neither birth-and-death nor extinction; it is neither that which is practiced nor that which is not practiced—this is called practicing the Dharma.
If one can practice all dharmas, this is called practicing the Dharma.
To practice the Dharma without any conception of "dharmas" is what is called practicing the Dharma.

He himself says: "I practice the Dharma not as one who practices [it conventionally]; for one who upholds the Dharma, it consists in completely eliminating all dharmas—that is the upholding of the Dharma."
"To practice without practicing anything regarding that which is practiced, and to thus honor and cultivate the Dharma—this is what is called 'the cultivation of the Dharma.
At that time, the Devaputra Aparivartana addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "If, O Great Sage!..."
Yet, within this context, those who do not practice with utmost sincerity are of a kind that does not honor [the teaching] and does not accord with the Dharma.
Why is this? Those who honor utmost sincerity have neither end nor death, and they do not abide upon the path of birth.
What is it that one should practice?
To abide upon the path of equanimity is itself practice.
Indeed, O Great Sage!
For one who practices equality, there are no erroneous dharmas. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are entirely equal and without distinction.
Thereupon, the Brahmā Citta asked the Devaputra Abhimukta-avivartin: "Do you practice this conduct? He replied:
“Brahmā! I shall practice accordingly.
Even if the World-Honored One were to speak of three practices, I would practice two things: that which is practiced, and once it has been practiced, there is no further practice.”
Furthermore, Brahmā!
I have already practiced the departure from all dualistic conduct, just as all dharmas are; my practice of all dharmas is likewise so.
To accord with the Dharma as it is and to practice as it is—this is what is called the practice of the Dharma.
He asked the devaputra again:
"Have you never before seen this buddha-field? He replied:
"I have never seen such a buddha-field before.
He asked again,
"Is it that you do not perceive this buddha-field?"
"There is neither correspondence nor non-correspondence; regarding that which is seen, there is nothing seen.
He replied, "Brahmā!"
"Now, my own body has neither thought nor non-thought, neither response nor non-response; I have both seen it and never seen it.
He then asked the Devaputra:
"What is it that you, O Devaputra, have seen?"
He replied: "I have never seen any noble sages or holy men; all ordinary people and the class of the foolish and ignorant neither cross over from the evil realms, nor do they fail to cross over."
Thus it is, Brahmā!
That which is equal attains liberation; this is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

It beholds what has never been seen before, yet it has no name and no destination. The eye does not discern or recognize; and so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—the mind likewise does not discern or recognize.
When that which is seen is as if it has no origin, then the eye is like the self; since there is no origin, there is nothing to be seen—this is the vision of equality.
