Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Fifteen: Bestowing the Prediction upon the Devaputra Abhimukta-avivartika (4).
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“O God among Gods! [...]”
Just as wherever a mani-jewel is placed, the light of that jewel is seen by the eyes of people in that very place;
so it is, World-Honored One!

These true persons, having fully practiced the inconceivable Dharma, roam with mastery and universally illuminate all things at will with the radiance of the Dharma-treasure. They immediately cultivate and manifest the primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi), and are capable of freely expounding eloquence. As for this freedom, they have no attachment or dependence regarding any phenomena, nor do they cling to "self" or "other."
One who possesses spontaneous eloquence has no opposition; they are never inverted and always attain mastery.
One who possesses spontaneous eloquence is pure regarding the past, does not grasp at the future, and does not perceive the present.
One who possesses spontaneous eloquence inspires faith in those without faith and delivers those who have not yet been liberated.
The one with unimpeded eloquence subdues all arrogance and transforms those who are self-important so that they attain decisive certainty;
the one with unimpeded eloquence ensures that no Māras can find an opportunity, and through his discernment, he transcends the works of Māra;

the one with unimpeded eloquence causes wholesome dharmas that have not yet been encouraged to arise, and once they have arisen, he advances them without neglect or forgetfulness; if afflictions should arise, he causes them to be eliminated, and before they have arisen, he prevents them from coming into being.
Those with unimpeded eloquence cause those bodhisattvas who have not yet donned the armor of virtue to don it; those who have donned it shall never regress.
Those with unimpeded eloquence do not sever the true Dharma and protect the authentic scriptures.
By means of this analogy regarding the principle of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), one is able to subdue all heterodox teachers. Why is this so?
Just as small beasts can never endure the roar of a lion, and upon seeing a lion cannot advance of their own accord—let alone enter its den or roam among its trees—so it is with these teachers.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
None of the followers of other teachings are able to endure the utterance of this unsurpassed lion’s roar.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Manifesting Non-Retrogression addressed Śakra, saying:
"What is meant by the so-called 'lion's roar' that you mentioned earlier, Kauśika?
What constitutes a lion's roar? He replied:
“Devaputra! That which regarding all phenomena is neither dependent nor attached and is beyond verbal expression—this is called seeing the lion’s roar.

To behold that which is without dependence and is silent is the lion’s roar; whereas one who relies upon or becomes attached to the practice of silence is merely the cry of a jackal, because they still have something to express regarding the perception of a state of equality.”
Furthermore, O Devaputra!
You should further explain: what is meant by "performing the lion's roar"?
The Devaputra replied:
"Kauśika, you should know that even for one who does not rely upon or cling to the Tathāgata, there is no verbal expression; how much more so for other diverse causes and conditions!
For this reason, the Dharma is called the Lion’s Roar;
to uphold the teaching of equality is termed the Lion’s Roar."
The exposition of a single chapter is called the Lion’s Roar;
hearing what is taught without fear is called the Lion’s Roar;
if one preaches the Dharma of the sutras as being neither arising nor ceasing and lacking any inherent nature, it is called the Lion’s Roar.
To dwell amidst the defilements without harboring fetters, neither joining nor dispersing—proclaiming such a Dharma is called the Lion’s Roar.

It is for this reason it is called the Lion’s Roar: if one can be single-mindedly devoted, reckoning neither of a person nor of a self, and understanding that all dharmas are merely conventional designations based on habitual usage.
That which is called the "Lion's Roar" is the single-minded proclamation of the Dharma of emptiness;
that which is called the "Lion's Roar" is the oral teaching that protects the True Dharma;
that which is called the "Lion's Roar" is the eradication of all the sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings, whereby one shall attain the Buddha-way and proclaim this teaching.
That which is called the "Lion's Roar" refers to the pure foundation of one’s thoughts regarding wealth and undertakings, knowing contentment and praising this teaching;
that which is called the "Lion's Roar" refers to dwelling in seclusion without discriminating among one's actions.

To establish the foundation of giving as the primary principle is the lion’s roar; not abandoning the prohibitions and precepts is the lion’s roar; maintaining an impartial mind toward both friends and enemies is the lion’s roar; neither forsaking what is distant nor approaching what is near is the lion’s roar; eliminating all worldly afflictions is the lion’s roar; and observing with equanimity through wisdom is the lion’s roar.

When the devaputra uttered this lion’s roar, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, and a great radiance shone universally throughout the world and all the celestial palaces.
Hundreds of thousands of devas and humans raised their voices in praise, saying:
"We have witnessed the Wheel of Dharma turn once again in Jambudvīpa, because of this son of heaven’s lion’s roar."

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately smiled with joy. When a Buddha who has attained perfect enlightenment smiles, immeasurable rays of light issue from his mouth—blue, yellow, red, white, black, purple, and crimson—illuminating countless, incalculable worlds of Buddhas so as to pervade them all without exception. Reaching upward to the Brahma Heaven, they completely eclipse the brilliance of the sun and moon; they circle the body three times and then re-enter through the crown of the head, vanishing instantly and without a trace.
The Brahma-deva Cittadhara rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke in verse:
“O One of peerless supernormal wisdom, Who universally knows all that exists,
And who fully discerns and understands The conduct of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.”
According to their inclinations and what they believe and rejoice in, they attain liberation through wisdom;
their minds are transcendent and extraordinary, and all are granted the prediction of enlightenment.
This is not the domain of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha’s wisdom is such as this: immeasurable and holding the infinite.
He clearly understands the minds of sentient beings; for what reason does he speak of their destinies?
To deliver and liberate sentient beings is a supreme excellence beyond compare.
According to the inclinations of his mind, he skillfully restrains his thoughts and eliminates defilement;
as his radiance emerges, it eclipses the sun, moon, Śakra, and Brahmā.
It shines through the Iron Ring Mountains and illuminates billions of Mount Sumerus.
I pray you will explain its essential meaning: by what cause is such joy inspired?
How is it that hatred and aversion are forever eliminated, and the Muni remains tranquil and serene?
With universal compassion, he gazes upon all within the heavens and the world.
Beholding the Buddha, one never tires; seeing his body brings benefit and peace.
The reason for his joyful smile is that he dwells securely in explaining the definitive meaning.
He discerns and examines all phenomena, as free and unimpeded as space.
Like clouds, mist, lightning, or flames, like a mass of foam or a phantom,
seeing all that exists as a dream or like the moon reflected in water—
excellent is this intended discourse; for what reason do you smile with joy?
Eliminating all conceptual perceptions and views, the Able One transcends and crosses over emptiness;
with all-encompassing wisdom he purifies defilements and remains forever detached from the clinging of thought.
Thus, there is no longing for the three realms; through meditative concentration, he abides in equanimity.
Therefore, exerting radiant light, he speaks only through correct discernment;
without letters or verbal expressions, and unattached to sounds or echoes,
he dwells in peace while preaching the sutras, having no longing for the dharmas of sentient beings.
He clearly understands each and every assembly, desiring to cause them to realize the Buddha’s wisdom.
Knowing the bases of psychic power, the faculties, and the powers, he delivers the most excellent and wondrous teaching.
The Buddha is the King of Physicians, who eliminates all suffering.
O Heroic One who has reached supreme peace, you deliver the foolish, the dull-witted, and the heedless;
your power and majesty surpass all fetters, and all people take refuge in you.
O Radiant One, Honored among Men and Gods, for what reason do you smile with joy?
The Buddha said to the Brahmā Citta-dhara:
"Do you see the Devaputra Avivartika? He replied:
“I see them, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā! The manifested non-regressing devaputra shall attain Buddhahood after thirty-two incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas; his name shall be Sumerupradīparāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His world shall be named Suvinīta, and his kalpa shall be named Viśuddhastava.”

That Buddha-land shall possess two precious substances, namely deep-blue lapis lazuli and purple-gold; it shall consist purely of a multitude of bodhisattvas who have subdued the hosts of Māra and their enemies. Their dwellings, clothing, food, and drink shall be like those of the sixth heaven, the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Nirmāṇarati).
The Tathāgata has diligently brought many to transformation and enlightenment; thereupon, the Brahmā Cittadhara addressed the Devaputra Abhimuktyavinivartanīya, saying:
"The Tathāgata has already bestowed upon you, noble sir, the prediction of your future enlightenment."

He replied: "The Tathāgata has already granted me the prediction [of enlightenment]. Just as one who is without origin grants a prediction to one without origin, and as it is with the Dharma-realm, so too is the prediction granted to me."
He replied: "Furthermore, because there is neither a fundamental basis nor a dharma-realm, there is no resolution. He answered:

“The Tathāgata bestows the prophecy of awakening within the fundamental dharma-realm where there is no dharma to be bestowed; all bodhisattvas are likewise thus, and they should not perceive any prophecy being bestowed.”
He asked again:

"Virtuous one, do you not abide by following the Perfectly Awakened One, purifying the holy life, and discerning with clear understanding as if you had received a prophecy from the Buddha? He replied:
“Brahmā! Those who have no further training in such categories as these are practicing the holy life (brahmacarya).
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'practicing the holy life through non-habituation'? He replied:
"One who does not habituate themselves to the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm—such as these practice the holy life."
Furthermore, Brahmā!

One who dwells in non-practice, does not dwell in a self, does not practice the notion of a person, does not practice the notion of a being, and does not practice the notion of a life—such as these are the companions who cultivate the holy life.
To state the essential point: to rely upon all phenomena while not becoming habituated to them—this is what is called "purely cultivating the holy life" (*brahmacarya*).
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'purely cultivating the holy life'?"
He replied, “This refers to the pure cultivation of the brahma-faring (brahmacarya) without dwelling in either of the two paths.
He asked again:
"If one does not abide in the two paths, upon what is one established?
He replied: "Not abiding in the two paths is precisely the establishment of the discourse on all dharmas."
"Why is this? Because that which has nothing to establish itself is what the worthy sages follow and practice to attain transcendence.
He asked again:
"What is it that one cultivates as the practice of the Way? He replied:

"There is one who practices by not falling into conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*) and yet not departing from activity; likewise, there is neither one who acts within phenomena (*dharma*) nor one who departs from phenomena. This is called practicing the Way with diligent compliance in accordance with reality."
He asked again:
"By what kind of practice does one perform the practice of the Path? He replied:

“Without seeing, without hearing, without thinking, and without knowing; without instruction, without attainment, and without realization—having no engagement with any phenomena whatsoever—is what is called practicing the path in accordance with the Way.”
He asked again:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s firm and vigorous diligence? He replied:

"If a bodhisattva does not perceive even a single phenomenon in their practice, nor does they perceive any variety of practices, this is called a bodhisattva’s firm and vigorous diligence in donning the armor of virtuous precepts."

To abide within the dharma-realm without causing any destruction—being without destruction, one has nothing to approach; neither departing from the dharma nor contradicting it, one perceives no afflictions and harbors no resentment. This is the foremost practice of a bodhisattva, which is diligence: to cultivate diligence by neither elevating nor deprecating any dharma.
"Furthermore, Brahmā!
To be without the causal conditions of body, without the causal conditions of speech, and without the causal conditions of mind—this is the foremost practice of diligence."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the devaputra Abhimukto-avivartika, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"It is as you have said.
He further addressed Citta-dhara: "So it is, Brahmā!"
That which the present Son of Heaven has spoken is the foremost practice of diligence; it is a state wherein there is no bodily action, no verbal action, and no mental action.
The Buddha told Brahmā:

"I recall that in the distant past, during ages long ago, I possessed the virtue of all-knowing tranquility; I cultivated diligence with single-minded devotion, reverently served [the worthy], dwelt in seclusion while studying extensively, and practiced compassion toward all classes of sentient beings. By what practices did I cultivate and manifest such diligent perseverance?"
The Tathāgata does not see [anyone] being granted the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment. Why is this?
Because they abide in the attachment to body, speech, and mind.

"At that time, Brahmā, having cultivated such physical form and diligently practiced this complete course of conduct as the devaputra has just described, shall in a future age behold the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and receive his prediction of enlightenment. In a future life, he shall become a Buddha, known by the names Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat, titled 'The Able One' (Śākyamuni)."

Therefore, Brahmā! If a bodhisattva wishes to swiftly receive the prediction of enlightenment, they should cultivate diligence according to this analogy, understanding all dharmas while remaining without any [discursive] activity.
Brahmā asked: "What is meant by the Blessed One having no activity?
The Blessed One replied:
“Ultimate equality, being perfectly even, empty, and non-existent, constitutes diligence.
“What is meant by ultimate equality, being perfectly even, empty, and non-existent, as diligence?”
He replied: "The past mind has ceased; the future has not yet arrived; the present does not abide. That which is extinguished does not arise again.

If one who has attained this has no thought of arising, such a dweller is eternally without a place of dwelling. As for that which constitutes the Dharma, if the True Dharma arises in equality, there is no arising. That which has no arising possesses no past, future, or present. If there is no going, coming, or the present, it is fundamentally pure and thus has no arising."
This, Brahmā, is ultimate equality:
to exert oneself with the perfect equanimity of emptiness and non-existence.
A bodhisattva who acts thus will swiftly receive the prediction of enlightenment, attain the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti), and become fully endowed with all practices.
The Buddha said to Brahmā:
"If a bodhisattva practices nothing at all regarding any phenomena, this is called giving;
if they do not maintain or guard any phenomena, this is called upholding the precepts."
If one does not give rise to thoughts regarding any phenomena, this is called patience;
if one regards all phenomena as being without causes or conditions, this is called diligence;
and if one views all phenomena with equanimity, this is called meditative concentration.
To have no conceptualization regarding all phenomena is called wisdom;
this is termed neither creating augmentation nor undergoing diminution, being without action and without non-action.

"Constantly practicing giving without expectation, upholding the prohibitive precepts with equanimity, cultivating patience so that both the internal and external are pure, carrying out diligence to full accomplishment, maintaining one-pointed concentration in meditation without any attachment, and revering wisdom without conceptualization."

A bodhisattva who thus fulfills the practice of patience performs all deeds universally yet remains entirely unattached; being unattached, they regard worldly phenomena with equanimity—neither rejoicing in gain nor grieving over loss, neither elated by praise nor dejected by blame, and remaining unmoved whether encountering pleasure or suffering.

"Even if one encounters this, remaining unmoving and unshakable—neither increasing nor decreasing, neither rejoicing nor grieving—one has already transcended all worldly phenomena. One does not suffer distress, nor affliction, nor tremble with fear; being without thought and without non-thought, there are no two things. Departing from all causes and conditions, one proceeds toward the dharma of non-duality. Falling into the two views, one gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and by awakening one's own mind, one transforms sentient beings. This, Brahmā, is the foremost diligence, for it attains patience through non-self (*anātman*); thus one turns toward the masses and enters into great compassion, gathering and protecting them wherever they are born."
When the Buddha had spoken these words on energetic exertion, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The Buddha bestowed upon them all the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that they would attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). They were all given the same name: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Dṛḍhavīrya (Firm and Strong Exertion). Each of them shall arise as a Buddha, a World-Honored One, in distinct buddha-fields.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Just as when great dragons wish to send rain, they rain upon the great ocean, so too it is with these true sons of noble family."

The God among Gods is like the great ocean; he manifests these forms and pours forth the great rain of Dharma. These great virtuous ones are likewise a vast sea, and their minds are also thus: they proclaim the rain of Dharma through the nature of reality.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"As you have said, it is not out of greed or jealousy that these great nāgas do not send rain upon Jambudvīpa; rather, it is because the ground of the realm of Jambudvīpa cannot withstand the falling drops of such heavy rain."

Suppose, Kāśyapa, that these great nāgas were to send down a great rain upon the world, such that the provinces, kingdoms, districts, towns, mountains, hills, and valleys of Jambudvīpa would be swept away and utterly submerged, like drifting leaves.
For this reason, the great dragon kings do not send down heavy rain upon Jambudvīpa.
In the same way, Kāśyapa,
these true men do not begrudge the rain of Dharma, yet they do not manifest the moisture of the Dharma for the sake of humans or other classes of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!

If there are vessels capable of containing the Buddha-dharma, these true sons of the Dharma will submerge their own intentions and awaken all sentient beings, manifesting the rain of Dharma according to their mental inclinations."

For example, Kāśyapa, when the dragons send down rain, they drop great drops like chariot wheels; the great ocean receives this heavy rain entirely, yet it does not consider itself satisfied, nor does it become full.

These noble beings are likewise: whether they hear the Dharma for a single eon or for hundreds of thousands of eons, they neither increase nor decrease in regard to all dharmas, nor do they consider them to be full.
“Kāśyapa, it is just as, for example,
all the waters from various places— the myriad rivers and four currents— that flow into the great ocean, once they have converged, become of a single taste, salty and bitter like salt.

These various noble beings, through their diverse voices, each expound different teachings so that all may hear the Dharma; yet upon hearing them, they all return to a single meaning: the flavor of liberation, which leads toward the flavor of emptiness and non-existence.

“Kāśyapa, it is just as, for example, within the great ocean there are jewels that are pure, stainless, clean, and flawless; because they do not receive water at improper times, nor do they receive impurities.
"These noble beings are likewise thus: pure and stainless, they do not harbor any flaws of resentment, weariness, or anger toward anything.
For example, Kāśyapa!"
Within the great ocean, it is exceedingly profound and deep; its bottom is difficult to reach and its boundaries are hard to limit.

These noble beings are likewise so: the holy wisdom they have realized is extremely deep and far-reaching; their minds enter into the mysterious, wondrous, and profound, being immeasurable and beyond the reach of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
“Kāśyapa, it is like this:
within the great ocean, there is stored an immeasurable and incalculable amount of water.

These true persons (satpuruṣa) are also like this; they accumulate and cultivate that which is beyond measure, for their perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) brings together all dharmas. Therefore, they are likened to the great ocean; those with such characteristics are called true persons.”
“Kāśyapa, it is just as, for example, within the great ocean there is an accumulation of immeasurable varieties of jewels.
These true persons (satpuruṣa) are also like this; they are naturally filled with the immeasurable dharma-jewels of various teachings.”
“Kāśyapa, it is like this:
within the great ocean there are three kinds of treasures—the treasure of the true body, the treasure of pure water, and the treasure of wealth and resources.”

These noble beings are likewise; when they preach the Dharma, they do so according to the faculties and origins of individuals, causing them to attain liberation from what their minds require to be freed, whether it be through the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or reaching the Great Vehicle.
“Kāśyapa, it is like this:
within the great ocean, as water gradually flows in, it becomes increasingly vast, deep, and wide.

In the same way, when a bodhisattva sets their mind upon the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and practices those supernormal knowledges, they gradually achieve accomplishment in the Great Path of the Sages.”
“Kāśyapa, it is just as, for example, the great ocean does not tolerate a corpse and does not dwell together with it. These true persons are also like this:

they do not cultivate the mind of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor do they share a common destination with them. They do not share a common destination with those who possess greed, envy, violation of precepts, resentment, indolence, or a mind of malice; nor do they share a common destination with those who practice indolence, distraction, or evil wisdom. They do not dwell or associate with those who hold views of a self, a person, a soul, or a life-span.”

“Kāśyapa, it is just as when the calamity of fire consumes and dries up the flowing streams, so that the great rivers, deep pools, and lakes are all parched away, and only then does the great ocean finally vanish without remainder.”
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!

When the True Dharma is propagated throughout all lands, one first practices the True Dharma through the application of giving; thereafter, one bestows it upon the ocean-like minds of the various awakened ones, for the True Dharma is that to which all such true beings (satpuruṣa) turn.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!

These true sons of noble family would rather sacrifice their own lives than abandon the True Dharma. As these true sons of noble family propagate the True Dharma, you should not form such views regarding them."

For example, suppose there were a wish-fulfilling jewel in the great ocean called Vajra; it would gather all manner of treasures and emerge for seven days, ascending as high as the Brahma Heaven and incinerating everything, including all the worlds of the trichiliocosm Buddha-fields until nothing remained, even extending to other regions.
The Buddha said,
“Kāśyapa! It has never happened that a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) would be burned or destroyed upon entering another world-system.”

In this way, Kāśyapa, these true persons exhaust all dharmas and cause them to flourish and arise; they establish the seven right dharmas so that the world may rely upon them, and then they travel again to other Buddha-fields.
What are the seven? They are:

following various non-Buddhist paths, following evil friends, falling into the practice of false views, mutually harming one another, accepting and falling into various [extreme] views, destroying the roots of all virtues, and failing to attain equanimity. These constitute the arousal and manifestation [of these states].

Regarding these seven dharmas, these true beings (satpuruṣa) are worthy recipients; they see that sentient beings fundamentally dwell in those Buddha-lands and never depart from the Buddhas, constantly beholding the Perfectly Awakened Ones and hearing the sūtras, while exhorting and transforming all beings to plant the roots of manifold virtues.
“Kāśyapa, it is like this:

just as countless beings with blood in their veins depend upon the great ocean to dwell and roam within it, so too do countless multitudes of people all come together and rely upon the bodhisattva; they dwell and roam together, returning to the same destination—the three realms of existence.”
What are these three?
Birth in the heavens, fulfillment among humans, and the attainment of nirvāṇa.
“For example, Kāśyapa, within the great ocean, the nāgas and asuras exercise their sovereign power.”
"These noble beings are likewise;
they universally subdue all hosts of Māra.
Thereupon, the elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the World-Honored One, asking:
“O God among Gods!
One might yet be able to measure the great ocean and reach its limits; but can these true sons of noble family be measured, so as to find their boundaries or depths?”
The World-Honored One replied:

"Kāśyapa! If one wishes to know all the atoms within the trichiliocosm, they may still be counted; however, the practice of these true persons of ultimate reality is inconceivable, and their final destination cannot be fathomed."
Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as the great ocean receives all waters, yet is never satiated."
Those who aspire to seek the Dharma are likewise thus: they delight in the true scriptures and are never satiated.
Just as the great ocean receives immeasurable waters, welcoming all that comes to it without ever refusing or turning them away.
Those who are wise and discerning are likewise thus; they do not consider themselves complete merely by means of their own wisdom.
The great ocean does not disdain muddy, turbid water; all clear streams likewise flow toward it.
The practitioner who follows this cultivation is likewise so: they do not receive any of the defilements of worldly toil.
They are like the great ocean, which cannot be measured; it is exceedingly vast and far-reaching, impossible to know all at once.
The ocean of wisdom and virtue is likewise so; though sentient beings cross over others, none can fully comprehend or explain it.
Within the great ocean, though there are various points of entry, the myriad rivers and fourfold streams merge into a single flavor.
Various kinds of people all come to listen to the Dharma; they all return to the One Vehicle, the scripture of shared meaning.
Not being of a single category, it is called a "sea"; those who came before have formed this sea, and thus it is established.
One who possesses fearlessness has aspirations such as these: for the sake of all sentient beings everywhere, they give rise to the resolve for the Way.
Like the great ocean, which is a repository where all manner of jewels are gathered, yet remains therein without any attachment.
The assembly of bodhisattvas is also like an accumulation of treasures, which, being made manifest, brings about the Three Jewels.
Just as the rivers and seas possess the Three Jewels, yet even those oceans have no conceptual thought.
The assembly of sages and realized ones preach the Dharma in this manner, using the three vehicles to guide and enlighten sentient beings.
Just as rivers and seas gradually increase in vastness, with all streams flowing back into them until they are completely filled.
The assembly of bodhisattvas, setting their minds upon the various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms for the sake of all living beings,
constantly abide in and practice them. Just as the great ocean does not accept corpses,
such is the nature of that ocean.
Establishing themselves as bodhisattvas, they seek the Way in this manner; yet they do not guard their bodies with worldly prudence, nor do they share the same destination [as ordinary beings].
Just as various treasures arise within the ocean, Mount Sumeru is the most sublime among them, standing firm and solid in its place.
When the conflagration at the end of an eon arises, it can never burn them; they will instead transcend and travel to other Buddha-worlds.
When the True Dharma perishes, it is likewise so: those who are strong in vigor and diligence will grasp and uphold it.
Having observed and seen that there is no one capable of being a vessel for the Dharma, he then departs for the abodes of other Buddhas in other directions.
Only when the mountain torrents, rivers, and streams have run dry, and even the springs and sources have been exhausted, will the waters of the great ocean finally evaporate.
When the conflagration at the end of the kalpa arises, it will be just like this; the great trichiliocosm will likewise collapse and be destroyed.
As for the multitudes of ordinary beings who dwell within the lands, even if the True Dharma has already completely vanished.
Those of courageous spirit protect the Dharma in this way, casting aside their bodies and not begrudging their lives.
Whether the Perfectly Awakened One is present in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, such as are their resolve and nature.
Purity is thus established;
that which the upholder of the Dharma should follow and cultivate is like billions of sentient beings relying upon the ocean as their refuge.

Because it is not of a single kind, there exists this state; its great renown and such aspirations—though all beings might attain universal liberation of mind, these [qualities] could still be measured.
One may discern and know them;
yet regarding the oceans of all that exists within the Buddha-worlds, the conduct of these beings cannot be individually discerned.

By seeing the treasury of the Buddha, one attains the divine eye; by hearing the treasury of the Dharma, one achieves the divine ear; by the treasury of the Noble Assembly, one attains non-retrogression; by the inexhaustible treasure-trove of Bodhisattvas and worthies, one attains the "Treasury of the Jewel-Palm"; by the treasury of physical form, one becomes endowed with the [thirty-two] marks; by the treasury of retinue, one’s followers do not disperse; by the uninterrupted treasure-trove, one attains *dhāraṇī*; by the treasury of resolve and mindfulness, one attains eloquence (*pratibhāna*); by the treasury of fearlessness, one gathers in all heterodox teachers; by the treasury of merit, sentient beings look up to and revere it; and by the treasury of noble wisdom, one universally obtains all the teachings of the Buddhas.

When the Buddha spoke this sutra, seventy-two koṭis of devas attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti); immeasurable multitudes of people all gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta), and an incalculable number of people were freed from outflows (āsravakṣaya) and attained liberation of mind.
The worthy Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What is the name of this sutra?
How should it be upheld?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This sūtra is named 'Equally Governing All Dharmas'; you should uphold it. It is also named 'Adorning the Buddha-dharma,' and further named 'The Questions of the Brahmā Citta-vatī and the Exposition by Samantamukha'; you should firmly uphold it."
Thus spoke the Buddha.

When the youth Viśeṣacintin, the Brahmā Cittadhara, the noble son Samantacārin, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, and the venerable Ānanda, along with the devas, humans, and asuras, heard what the Buddha had taught, they were all filled with joy.
